title: Habit Challenge Cards
content:
Habit Challenge Cards# Each card is a scenario. Your team designs the system that solves it, using the four laws — make it obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying. For the cards under Breaking a Bad Habit, invert them: make it invisible, unattractive, hard, and unsatisfying.
Building a Good Habit# Daily Reading Habit# Your team is handed a fresh grad who reads zero pages a week. Design a system that gets them into a sustainable daily reading habit.
Fitness / Movement Habit# Your team is handed a fresh grad who hasn’t exercised since college and dreads the idea of ‘working out.’ Design a system that gets them moving most days without relying on motivation.
English Speaking / Public Communication# Your team is handed a fresh grad who freezes up speaking in meetings or in English generally. Design a system that builds daily speaking reps into their week.
Personal Finance / Budgeting# Your team is handed a fresh grad who’s never tracked a rupee and is already living paycheck to paycheck. Design a system that gets them budgeting and saving automatically.
Journaling / Reflection Habit# Your team is handed a fresh grad who’s tried journaling five times and quit five times. Design a system that makes daily reflection stick.
Consistent Sleep / Wake-Up Routine# Your team is handed a fresh grad who sleeps at random hours and starts every day rushed. Design a system that locks in a consistent wake time.
Skill-Building Habit# Your team is handed a fresh grad who wants to learn a new skill ’eventually’ but never opens the course. Design a system that turns ’eventually’ into daily practice.
Networking / Relationship-Building Habit# Your team is handed a fresh grad who never reaches out to people unless they need something. Design a system for staying in touch and building their network as a habit, not a scramble.
Breaking a Bad Habit# Sugar / Junk Food# Your team is handed a fresh grad who reaches for sugar every time they’re stressed or bored. Design a system that breaks the reach, using the inverted four laws.
Instagram / TikTok Doomscroll# Your team is handed a fresh grad losing 90+ minutes a night to the scroll. Design a system that makes the habit invisible, hard, and costly.
Procrastination on Starting Tasks# Your team is handed a fresh grad who always finds something else to do before starting real work. Design a system that kills the delay at the two-minute mark.
Late-Night Screen Use / Poor Sleep Hygiene# Your team is handed a fresh grad who’s on their phone in bed until 1am every night. Design a system that removes the cue instead of asking for willpower.
Impulse Spending# Your team is handed a fresh grad who buys on impulse every time an ad or sale notification hits. Design a system that adds friction and real cost to the impulse.
Negative Self-Talk / Comparison Spiral# Your team is handed a fresh grad who spirals into self-criticism after every small mistake or every scroll through someone else’s highlight reel. Design a system that interrupts the spiral before it takes hold.
Notification-Driven Distraction at Work# Your team is handed a fresh grad who can’t hold focus for 20 minutes without checking a ping. Design a system that makes deep, uninterrupted work the path of least resistance.
Skipping Breakfast / Erratic Eating# Your team is handed a fresh grad who skips breakfast most days and crashes by 11am. Design a system that makes eating on schedule the easy default.

title: Particle Detector 2
content:
Extension — Scan in Two Directions# Our particle detector has so far been scanning from left to right and back again.
That means we have been thinking about ranges along the horizontal direction.
But our region of space has two dimensions.
Why should we only scan horizontally?
A particle detector could also scan from top to bottom.
A New Direction# Add another scanner to your simulation.
This scanner should move vertically.
It should start at the top of the region, move towards the bottom, and then bounce back towards the top.
Just like the other scanners, it is a range.
The difference is that this range now describes a position along the vertical direction rather than the horizontal direction.
Until now, a range might have looked like this:
start end | | v v +----------------+ | | | | | | +----------------+The range extends across the entire height of the screen.
Our new range works the other way around:
start | v +-------+ | | | | | | | | +-------+ ^ | endThis range extends across the entire width of the screen.
The important idea has not changed.
It still has:
a start; an end; a width; a position; movement; and the possibility of overlapping another range. Only the direction has changed.
A Horizontal Particle Field# We also need something for the new scanner to detect.
Add a particle field that is represented horizontally.
The existing particle fields occupy the full height of the screen:
+-----+ | | | | | | | | +-----+The new particle field should occupy the full width of the screen:
+-----------------------------+ | | +-----------------------------+It therefore represents a range along the vertical axis.
When the vertical scanner overlaps this particle field, it should turn red.
When it is not overlapping the field, it should remain white.
Your Task# Extend your program so that you now have:
the two scanners that scan horizontally; the horizontal particle fields; a new scanner that scans vertically; a new particle field that is also represented vertically; overlap detection between the new scanner and the new particle field. The new scanner should:
move from the top towards the bottom; bounce when it reaches the edge; move back towards the top; continue doing this; turn red when it overlaps the particle field; remain white when it does not. The existing scanners should continue working exactly as they did before.
Do not break something that already works while adding something new.
Think About the Range# There is an important question here.
Your overlap function already knows how to answer a question about two ranges.
Do you need a completely different idea for vertical ranges?
Think about what the overlap function actually knows.
Does it know that a range represents something horizontal?
Or does it simply receive a start and an end and determine whether two ranges overlap?
The meaning of the range has changed.
The underlying idea has not.
Try to keep that distinction in mind while you work.
Organize Your Code# This extension is also an opportunity to look carefully at the organization of your program.
You now have different kinds of things:
horizontal scanners; a vertical scanner; horizontal particle fields; vertical particle fields; movement; drawing; overlap detection. As you add the new behaviour, think about where each piece of code belongs.
Do not simply keep adding code to update() or draw() because it is convenient.
Ask yourself:
What is this piece of code responsible for?
and:
Does this belong here, or should it be part of a function?
You may discover that some of the code you wrote in the earlier steps can now be improved.
That is expected.
Good programs often become clearer as you understand the problem better.
Test It# Do not only test the particular values you have been given.
Change things.
Try:
moving the horizontal particle field; changing its size; changing the vertical scanner’s speed; changing the scanner’s width; making the particle field very small; making the particle field very large; putting the particle field near an edge; putting it in the middle. Your program should continue to work.
The same idea should apply to the existing horizontal scanners too.
Commit Your Work# When the extension is working:
Test it with several different values. Look through your code carefully. Refactor anything that needs improving. Make sure your functions have clear responsibilities. Check your variable and function names. Commit your changes. Push your commit to Git. Extension Checklist# Before you finish, go through the checklist from the main assignment again.
Do your functions rely on as few global variables as possible? Are your variable names clear? Are your function names clear? Where should your variables and functions live? Are your declarations happening in the right place? Are they in the right file? Have you removed unnecessary variables? Have you removed unnecessary functions? Have you tested your code with a variety of values? Can you extract any more useful functions? Have you made updates in the right function? Have you accidentally duplicated code that could be shared? Does the original horizontal scanning behaviour still work? Does the new vertical scanner stay inside the region? Does the vertical scanner correctly detect the horizontal particle field? Does the overlap logic still work for different ranges? Does your code still make sense when you read it from beginning to end? Finally, stop and think about what you have built.
You started with a scanner moving across a screen.
You then modeled the scanner as a range, modeled objects in space as ranges, and wrote a general rule for determining whether two ranges overlap.
Now the same idea works in another direction.
The problem was not really about horizontal strips or vertical strips.
It was about ranges and relationships between ranges.

title: Simple JS Practice
content:
JavaScript Practice# Solve the following problems in JavaScript.
You have not learned traditional loops yet, so do not use for, while, or similar loops. Use recursion whenever you need to repeat an operation.
Write a separate function for each problem.
1. Simple Interest# Write a function that calculates simple interest.
The function should take:
principal amount rate of interest time and return the simple interest.
For example:
simpleInterest(1000, 5, 2) → 100 2. Compound Interest# Write a function that calculates compound interest.
The function should take:
principal amount rate of interest number of years and return the compound interest.
For example, if ₹1000 is invested at 10% per year for 2 years, the final amount is ₹1210.
3. Print Even Numbers# Write a function that prints all the even numbers from 1 up to a given number.
For example:
printEvenNumbers(10) 2 4 6 8 10 4. Decimal to Binary# Write a function that converts a positive decimal integer into its binary representation.
For example:
decimalToBinary(10) → 1010 decimalToBinary(7) → 111 decimalToBinary(16) → 10000 5. Factorial# Write a function that calculates the factorial of a number.
For example:
factorial(5) → 120Remember:
5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 6. Nth Fibonacci Term# Write a function that returns the nth term of the Fibonacci sequence.
Use this definition:
F(0) = 0 F(1) = 1 F(n) = F(n - 1) + F(n - 2)For example:
fibonacci(0) → 0 fibonacci(1) → 1 fibonacci(6) → 8 7. Fibonacci Series# Write a function that prints the first n terms of the Fibonacci sequence.
For example:
fibonacciSeries(7) 0 1 1 2 3 5 8 8. Is Prime?# Write a function that determines whether a number is prime.
For example:
isPrime(7) → true isPrime(12) → falseA prime number is a number greater than 1 that has no divisors other than 1 and itself.
9. Find All Primes# Write a function that prints all prime numbers between 1 and a given number.
For example:
findAllPrimes(10) 2 3 5 7You will need to make use of your isPrime function.
10. First Prime Above# Write a function that finds the first prime number greater than a given number.
For example:
firstPrimeAbove(10) → 11 firstPrimeAbove(20) → 23 11. HCF# Write a function that finds the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of two numbers.
For example:
hcf(12, 18) → 6 hcf(20, 30) → 10 12. LCM# Write a function that finds the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of two numbers.
For example:
lcm(4, 6) → 12 lcm(5, 7) → 35 13. Armstrong Number# Write a function that determines whether a number is an Armstrong number.
For a three-digit number, an Armstrong number is a number whose value is equal to the sum of the cubes of its digits.
For example:
153 = 1³ + 5³ + 3³Therefore, 153 is an Armstrong number.
Your function should return true or false.
14. Palindrome# Write a function that determines whether a number is a palindrome.
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards.
For example:
121 → true 123 → false 15. Leap Year# Write a function that determines whether a given year is a leap year.
For example:
isLeapYear(2024) → true isLeapYear(2023) → false 16. Prime Factors# Write a function that prints all the prime factors of a number.
For example:
primeFactors(12) 2 2 3Another example:
primeFactors(60) 2 2 3 5 17. Square Root# Write a function that calculates the square root of a number.
Do not use Math.sqrt().
For example:
squareRoot(25) → 5 squareRoot(49) → 7Think carefully about how you could approximate the answer when the number is not a perfect square.
18. Sum of an Arithmetic Progression# Write a function that calculates the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic progression.
The function should take:
the first term the common difference the number of terms For example:
sumOfAP(2, 3, 5) → 40because:
2 + 5 + 8 + 11 + 14 = 40

title: Particle Detector
content:
Scanning for Particles# Imagine that we have sent a particle detector into space.
The detector is looking at a small region of space around it. It moves from one side of the region to the other, scanning for particles as it goes.
Our job is to build a simulation of this detector.
You will build the simulation in several steps. Each step adds one small idea to the previous one.
Do not try to build the whole thing at once.
After you have successfully completed each step, commit your work and push it to Git before moving on.
You should also take a moment at the end of each step to look at your code. Ask yourself whether it is still organized sensibly. If you have duplicated something, introduced a variable in the wrong place, or have a function that is becoming difficult to understand, this is a good time to fix it.
The Region of Space# Your simulation will show a rectangular region of space.
For simplicity, we will represent this region using the entire height of the screen.
For example, if your window is 300 pixels wide and 200 pixels high, the region of space is:
0 300 +----------------------------------------+ | | | | | | | | | | | | +----------------------------------------+ 200The important dimension for our problem is the horizontal dimension.
We will represent things in space as ranges.
A range has a start and an end.
For example:
start end | | v v +-----------------+ | range | +-----------------+If a range starts at 100 and ends at 150, it occupies every position between 100 and 150.
Visually, we will draw this as a vertical strip extending across the entire height of the screen:
100 150 | | v v +---------------+ | | | RANGE | | | | | +---------------+We are therefore using the horizontal position to represent our range, while the range occupies the entire height of the screen.
This will make it easier to see what is happening.
Step 1 — Build the Scanner# Start with just the particle detector.
The detector itself is a range.
Give it a width. For example, you might make it 20 pixels wide.
It should start somewhere on the left side of the region and move horizontally.
When it reaches one edge, it should change direction.
When it reaches the other edge, it should change direction again.
The result should look something like this:
The scanner should continue moving back and forth for the duration of your program.
Your task# Make the scanner:
move horizontally; reverse direction when it reaches an edge; remain completely inside the region of space; occupy the full height of the screen. You will need to work out how to represent the scanner’s position, width and direction.
You already know enough Raylib to do this.
Do not move on until the scanner works.
Then:
Review your code. Refactor anything that is unnecessarily complicated. Commit your changes. Push your commit to Git. Step 2 — A Particle Field# Our detector is now moving through space.
But there is nothing to detect yet.
Let’s introduce a particle field.
For now, imagine that a group of particles occupies a fixed range of space.
Draw one blue range somewhere in the region.
For example:
blue range | v +---------------+ | | | | | | +---------------+The blue range should also occupy the entire height of the screen.
Use approximately:
start: 100 width: 50 The scanner should continue behaving exactly as it did in Step 1.
It should move back and forth, while the blue range remains stationary.
Your task# Add the blue particle field without breaking the scanner.
Think carefully about how you represent the particle field.
It is a range.
That means you should be able to describe it using its start and end.
It should not matter that we have chosen these particular values. Your program should work if the particle field is moved somewhere else or given a different width.
Then:
Look over your code. Consider whether your new variables are in the right place. Consider whether anything should be extracted into a function. Commit your changes. Push your commit to Git. Step 3 — Detect an Overlap# Now we have a problem worth solving.
The detector is moving through the region of space.
At some point, the detector will encounter the particle field.
When the detector and the particle field occupy some of the same space, we say that their ranges overlap.
For example:
Scanner: +----------------+ | | +----------------+ Particle field: +------------------+ | | +------------------+ <--- overlap --->We want the scanner to tell us when this happens.
When there is no overlap, the scanner should be white.
When there is an overlap, the scanner should become red.
There is something important to notice here.
The scanner is itself a range.
The particle field is also a range.
So the question we are asking is:
Do these two ranges overlap?
You need to write a function that answers this question.
It should receive the information needed to describe the two ranges and return whether they overlap.
Do not make this function specific to the particular values you chose for your particle field.
It should work for any two ranges.
For example, it should work if one range is:
100 to 150and another is:
130 to 180But it should also work if you change them to completely different values.
Both ways# There is another important property you should test.
If range A overlaps range B, then range B also overlaps range A.
In other words, your overlap test must work both ways.
Test both of these situations:
scanner → particle fieldand:
particle field → scannerThe answer should be the same.
Think carefully about the different positions the two ranges can have.
What happens when:
they are completely separate? they just touch? one is partly inside the other? one completely contains the other? they are exactly the same range? You do not need to create a complicated test framework for this. Change the values in your program and observe what happens.
Your task# Make the scanner change color:
white when the two ranges do not overlap; red when they do overlap. Do not hard-code the answer for the particular positions you have chosen.
Your overlap function should work for arbitrary ranges.
Then:
Test it with several different positions and widths. Check the overlap in both directions. Look at your code and see whether anything can be simplified. Commit your changes. Push your commit to Git. Step 4 — Another Particle Field# Space is rarely so simple.
Let’s introduce another particle field.
You should now have two blue ranges.
For example, you can use approximately:
First field: start = 100 width = 50 Second field: start = 200 width = 5The exact values are not important.
Your program should work with other values too.
The scanner should behave exactly as it did before.
It should:
move back and forth; turn red when it overlaps either particle field; remain white when it overlaps neither. Notice that we now have two possible things for the scanner to detect.
The scanner is asking:
Do I overlap the first range or the second range?
You will need to decide how to organize this in your program.
Do not simply duplicate large pieces of code.
Think about the functions you already have.
Could one function be responsible for determining whether two ranges overlap?
Could another part of your program use that function to determine whether the scanner has detected something?
Then:
Test the scanner against both particle fields. Try different positions and widths. Refactor anything that has become repetitive. Commit your changes. Push your commit to Git. Step 5 — Two Particle Detectors# Our region of space is getting larger.
We are now going to use two particle detectors.
Divide the region into two halves.
The first detector is responsible for scanning the left half.
The second detector is responsible for scanning the right half.
For a 300-pixel-wide region, that means:
150 | v +--------------------+--------------------+ | | | | Scanner 1 | Scanner 2 | | | | | ← → | ← → | | | | +--------------------+--------------------+ 0 150 300Both scanners should move back and forth.
The first scanner must remain in the left half.
The second scanner must remain in the right half.
Give the two scanners different speeds.
For example, one might move one pixel per frame while the other moves two pixels per frame.
Both scanners should otherwise behave in the same way.
They are both ranges.
They have the same kind of representation.
They have the same kind of movement.
They should also use the same visual language:
white when they are not overlapping a particle field; red when they are overlapping a particle field. Your task# Modify your program so that it contains two scanners.
Make sure each scanner:
has its own position; has its own movement; stays within its own half of the region; moves at a different speed from the other scanner; detects the particle fields using the same overlap logic. Try changing the width of the window.
Try changing the speeds.
Try changing the particle fields.
Your program should still behave sensibly.
There is an important organizational question here:
Do you need two different functions to move the two scanners?
The scanners behave in the same way.
The things that are different are their values.
Think carefully about what should be shared and what should be different.
When you have finished:
Test both scanners thoroughly. Try different speeds. Try different particle-field positions and widths. Check that each scanner stays inside its own half. Refactor your code. Commit your changes. Push your commit to Git. Code Review# You have now built the complete simulation.
Before you consider the assignment finished, go through your code carefully.
Do not treat this as optional cleanup.
Part of programming is being able to look at a program you have just written and improve its organization.
Use the following checklist.
Checklist# Functions# Do your functions rely on as few global variables as possible? Can any information be passed into a function instead of being taken from a global variable? Can you further extract useful functions out of your code? Does each function have a clear responsibility? Are you updating things in the right function? Names# Are your variable names clear? Are your function names clear? If someone read the name without reading the implementation, would they have a reasonable idea what it represents? Are you using the same terminology consistently throughout the program? Organization# Where should each variable be? Where should each function be? Are your variable declarations happening in the right place? Are your function declarations happening in the right place? Are things in the right file? Have you accidentally put something in main that belongs somewhere else? Have you accidentally put something in sketch that belongs somewhere else? Unnecessary Code# Can you get rid of any unnecessary variables? Can you get rid of any unnecessary functions? Have you accidentally duplicated code? Is there code that was useful while experimenting but is no longer needed? Testing# Have you tested your code with a variety of values? Have you changed the positions of the particle fields? Have you changed their widths? Have you changed the scanner widths? Have you changed the scanner speeds? Have you tested ranges that are completely separate? Have you tested ranges that partially overlap? Have you tested one range completely inside another? Have you tested ranges that just touch? Refactoring# Can you make the program simpler? Can you make the program easier to understand? Can you further extract functions? Are related things kept together? Have you made updates in the right function? Does your code still make sense if you read it from the beginning? Finally, run your program one more time.
Watch the scanners.
Watch the particle fields.
Make sure you understand why the scanner turns red.
If you can explain why the overlap function gives the answer it does for every situation you have tested, you are done.
I deliberately left the overlap algorithm completely unspecified. The visual progression should give them enough information to discover the condition themselves, while Step 3 makes the key conceptual point explicit: both things are ranges, and overlap is a relationship between two ranges.

title: Template
content:
Modules and a Raylib Template# So far, each Raylib program you have written has lived in a single file.
We have already started organizing that file into functions:
function setup() {} function update() {} function draw() {} function loop() { while (!r.WindowShouldClose()) { update(); draw(); } } function main() { setup(); loop(); } main();This gives different parts of the program different responsibilities.
But there is another kind of organization available to us.
We can separate our program into different files.
To understand how, we first need to learn about modules.
A Small Module# Create a directory:
~/workspace/modulesInside it, create two files:
modules/ ├── main.js └── numbers.jsPut this in numbers.js:
function double(n) { return n * 2; } module.exports = { double, };There is one new thing here:
module.exports = { double, };We are saying that the function double should be available to other files.
We say that we are exporting double.
Now go to main.js.
Write:
const numbers = require("./numbers"); console.log(numbers);Run the program.
Look carefully at what is printed.
Now change it to:
const numbers = require("./numbers"); console.log(typeof numbers);What do you get?
You should see:
objectrequire() returns something.
In this case, it returns an object.
The object contains the things that numbers.js exported.
So we can write:
const numbers = require("./numbers"); console.log(numbers.double(5));This should print:
10There are two sides to what just happened.
In numbers.js:
module.exports = { double, };we export something.
In main.js:
const numbers = require("./numbers");we require that module.
Then:
numbers.double(5);uses something provided by the module.
More Than One Function# Add another function to numbers.js:
function double(n) { return n * 2; } function square(n) { return n * n; } module.exports = { double, square, };Now try:
const numbers = require("./numbers"); console.log(numbers.double(5)); console.log(numbers.square(5));The object returned by require() now gives us both functions:
numbers ├── double └── squareA module can provide several things to another part of our program.
A Function We Have Already Reused# Think back to the first Raylib exercises.
You had to centre a rectangle in the window.
You eventually wrote a function similar to:
function calcOffset(outer, inner) { return (outer - inner) / 2; }Then you had to centre one rectangle inside another rectangle.
The same calculation appeared again.
Then you scaled a rectangle and centred it.
Again, you needed the same calculation.
We solved one problem already.
Instead of repeating:
(outer - inner) / 2;everywhere, we put the calculation in a function.
Now suppose you have several different programs:
01_center_rectangle.js 02_center_rectangle_in_rectangle.js 03_scale_and_center.jsEach program could contain its own copy of calcOffset().
But now we are repeating something again.
Not the calculation this time.
The function itself.
Reusing a Function Across Programs# Create a file called:
geometry.jsPut the function in it:
function calcOffset(outer, inner) { return (outer - inner) / 2; } module.exports = { calcOffset, };Now another file can use it:
const geometry = require("./geometry"); const x = geometry.calcOffset(400, 200); console.log(x);The function no longer needs to belong to one particular Raylib program.
It belongs to geometry.js.
Any program that needs the calculation can require the module.
This gives us another kind of reuse.
First we learned:
repeated calculation ↓ functionNow we have:
useful function ↓ module ↓ used by different programsA function lets us reuse a computation.
A module lets us reuse functions across files.
A Small Library# We have just created a module called geometry.js.
It contains a function that is useful to more than one program:
function calcOffset(outer, inner) { return (outer - inner) / 2; } module.exports = { calcOffset, };There is another word you will hear when talking about reusable code:
library.
A library is code that has been written so that other programs can use it.
Our geometry.js is a very small library.
It is also a module.
These words are related, but they are not quite the same thing.
A module is a unit of code that can be used by another part of a program.
A library is reusable code intended to be used by other programs.
For now, you don’t need to worry too much about the distinction.
Just remember:
module ↓ a reusable unit of code library ↓ reusable code that programs can useOur geometry library might eventually contain several useful functions:
function calcOffset(outer, inner) { return (outer - inner) / 2; } function distance(x1, y1, x2, y2) { // ... } function intersects(a, b) { // ... } module.exports = { calcOffset, distance, intersects, };Different programs can require the library and use whichever functions they need.
You have already been using a library without thinking about it.
When we write:
const r = require("raylib");we are requiring the Raylib library.
Raylib provides us with functions for creating windows, drawing shapes, reading input, and many other things.
So there is nothing mysterious about a library.
It is simply useful code that someone else has written and made available for our programs to use.
We will build some small libraries of our own as we continue.
Back to Our Raylib Skeleton# Now return to the skeleton we have been using.
We previously separated the program into:
setup update draw loop mainThese functions do not all have the same responsibility.
setup() prepares our particular program.
update() changes our particular program.
draw() displays our particular program.
But loop() is different.
It is the machinery that repeatedly does this:
update(); draw();And main() is the machinery that starts everything.
There is a useful boundary here.
We can put the code that describes our particular drawing or animation in one file.
We will call that file:
sketch.jsAnd we can put the machinery that runs the sketch in:
main.jsOur program will become:
main.js sketch.jsCreating sketch.js# Start with:
const r = require("raylib"); function setup() {} function update() {} function draw() {} module.exports = { setup, update, draw, };There is nothing surprising here anymore.
sketch.js contains three functions.
It exports them.
Therefore another file can require sketch.js and receive an object containing those functions.
Using the Sketch# Now create main.js.
Start with:
const sketch = require("./sketch"); console.log(typeof sketch);What should this print?
Think about it before running the program.
Run it.
You should see:
objectNow we can access:
sketch.setup; sketch.update; sketch.draw;And we can call them:
sketch.setup(); sketch.update(); sketch.draw();Our functions are in one file.
The code using them is in another.
Rebuilding the Loop# Now we can write:
const sketch = require("./sketch"); function loop() { while (sketch.running()) { sketch.update(); sketch.draw(); } }There is a problem.
We haven’t written running() yet.
That is deliberate.
The loop should not need to know that we are using Raylib.
Think about what the loop actually needs to know.
It needs to know:
Should I keep running?
It doesn’t need to know why.
The answer to that question belongs to the sketch.
So add this to sketch.js:
function running() { return !r.WindowShouldClose(); }And export it:
module.exports = { running, setup, update, draw, };Now main.js can simply ask:
while (sketch.running()) { sketch.update(); sketch.draw(); }Notice something important.
main.js does not contain:
require("raylib");It does not know about:
r.WindowShouldClose();It doesn’t know that there is a Raylib window at all.
It only knows that the sketch can tell it whether it should keep running.
This is a useful boundary.
One More Part: Teardown# There is one part of our program that we have not given a name yet.
At the beginning of the program we do some work once:
setup();Then we repeatedly update and draw:
loop();Eventually the loop finishes.
The program needs to clean things up.
We will call this:
teardown();For now, it is very small:
function teardown() { r.CloseWindow(); }Add it to sketch.js.
The complete file now looks like this:
const r = require("raylib"); function running() { return !r.WindowShouldClose(); } function setup() {} function update() {} function draw() {} function teardown() { r.CloseWindow(); } module.exports = { running, setup, update, draw, teardown, };Why create a whole function for one line?
For the same reason that we created an empty update() earlier.
We are creating a place for a particular responsibility.
Today teardown means:
r.CloseWindow();Later a program may have other things that need to be cleaned up or finished before it exits.
We now have a place for them.
Our program has a lifecycle:
setup ↓ loop ↓ teardownInside the loop:
update → draw ↑ ↓ └───────┘setup() happens once at the beginning.
update() and draw() happen repeatedly.
teardown() happens once at the end.
main()# Now we can write main():
function main() { sketch.setup(); loop(); sketch.teardown(); }And finally:
main();Our complete main.js is now:
const sketch = require("./sketch"); function loop() { while (sketch.running()) { sketch.update(); sketch.draw(); } } function main() { sketch.setup(); loop(); sketch.teardown(); } main();Look at this file carefully.
There is nothing Raylib-specific in it.
main.js does not import Raylib.
It does not create a window.
It does not close a window.
It does not draw anything.
It does not know what kind of program it is running.
It only knows about the lifecycle of a program:
setup ↓ running? ↓ update → draw ↑ ↓ └───────┘ ↓ teardownThe sketch provides the details.
This is a much more useful separation than simply putting different functions into different files.
Warning: Keep Your State in the Sketch# There is one important rule to remember as you move your existing programs into this structure.
Do not put your program’s variables in main.js.
For example, suppose your program has a rectangle that moves:
let x = 100; let y = 100; let speed = 2;It may be tempting to put these variables in main.js because main.js is running the program.
Don’t.
These variables describe the state of your sketch.
They belong in sketch.js:
const r = require("raylib"); let x = 100; let y = 100; let speed = 2; function running() { return !r.WindowShouldClose(); } function setup() { // ... } function update() { x += speed; } function draw() { // ... } function teardown() { r.CloseWindow(); } module.exports = { running, setup, update, draw, teardown, };main.js should remain concerned with the lifecycle of the program:
setup ↓ running? ↓ update ↓ draw ↓ running? ↓ ... ↓ teardownThe variables that describe what is happening belong to the sketch.
A useful question to ask is:
Does this variable describe the machinery that runs the program, or does it describe the thing I am building?
If it describes the thing you are building, it belongs in sketch.js.
This keeps main.js generic.
You should be able to take the same main.js and use it with a completely different sketch without changing it.
That is one of the reasons we separated the files in the first place.
Put Something in the Sketch# An empty sketch is not very interesting.
Move one of your existing Raylib programs into this structure.
For example, sketch.js might contain the state for a rectangle:
const r = require("raylib"); const screenWidth = 400; const screenHeight = 400; const FPS = 60; let rectWidth = 200; let rectHeight = 200; function running() { return !r.WindowShouldClose(); } function setup() { r.InitWindow(screenWidth, screenHeight, "Rectangle"); r.SetTargetFPS(FPS); } function update() { rectWidth++; rectHeight--; } function draw() { // draw the rectangle } function teardown() { r.CloseWindow(); } module.exports = { running, setup, update, draw, teardown, };Fill in draw() yourself.
You have already solved this problem.
And remember: if you need your centering calculation, you already know how to move that calculation into geometry.js and require it.
A Useful Structure# We now have three different kinds of code.
main.jscontains the machinery that runs our program.
sketch.jscontains the particular thing we are currently building.
geometry.jscan contain useful geometry calculations that several programs may need.
These files exist because the code has different responsibilities.
Do not separate code into files merely because you can.
Ask:
What belongs together?
and:
What might be useful somewhere else?
The boundaries come first.
The files follow those boundaries.
We Keep Writing the Same main.js# There is something interesting about main.js.
Look at it again:
const sketch = require("./sketch"); function loop() { while (sketch.running()) { sketch.update(); sketch.draw(); } } function main() { sketch.setup(); loop(); sketch.teardown(); } main();Suppose tomorrow you want to write a program that draws circles.
Will main.js change?
Probably not.
Suppose you want to animate a rectangle.
Will main.js change?
Probably not.
Suppose you want to draw several moving shapes.
Again, main.js probably does not need to change.
We have discovered some code that we will use again and again.
We could copy it manually every time.
But we can do something better.
We can make ourselves a template.
Create a Raylib Template# Create a new directory:
mkdir ~/workspace/raylib_templateInside it, create:
raylib_template/ ├── main.js ├── sketch.js └── geometry.jsPut the reusable main.js into the template.
Your sketch.js should contain the structure:
const r = require("raylib"); function running() { return !r.WindowShouldClose(); } function setup() { // prepare the sketch } function update() { // change the state } function draw() { // draw the current state } function teardown() { r.CloseWindow(); } module.exports = { running, setup, update, draw, teardown, };And geometry.js can begin with the useful calculation we have already discovered:
function calcOffset(outer, inner) { return (outer - inner) / 2; } module.exports = { calcOffset, };Your template is now a small program with most of its structure already in place.
Notice the division:
main.js | | knows only about the lifecycle ↓ sketch.js | | knows about Raylib ↓ Raylibmain.js doesn’t care what is happening inside the sketch.
This is useful because the machinery for running a sketch can now remain unchanged while the sketch itself changes.
Starting a New Project# Suppose you want to start a new project called:
moving_circleYou do not need to create all these files again.
You already have a starting point.
Run:
cp -R ~/workspace/raylib_template ~/workspace/moving_circleNow look inside:
moving_circle/ ├── main.js ├── sketch.js └── geometry.jsYou have a complete copy of the template.
Go into the new project:
cd ~/workspace/moving_circleNow start working on sketch.js.
Fill in:
setup(); update(); draw(); teardown();You should usually not need to rewrite main.js.
If you need the centering calculation, use the function in geometry.js.
If you discover another useful geometry calculation that belongs there, you can add it.
What We Have Done# There are several ideas connected here.
We started with a calculation:
(outer - inner) / 2We wanted to reuse it, so we made a function.
Then we wanted to reuse that function in different files, so we made a module.
Then we noticed that our Raylib skeleton already had useful boundaries:
setup update draw loop mainWe used modules to make those boundaries visible in our files.
We also added two new ideas:
running() teardown()running() hides the question of how we know whether the program should continue.
teardown() gives us a place to clean things up when the program finishes.
So the life of our program is now:
setup ↓ running? ↓ update → draw ↑ ↓ └───────┘ ↓ teardownFinally, we noticed that much of this structure does not change from one program to another.
So we made a template.
There is a pattern here:
repeat a calculation ↓ make a function ↓ reuse the function ↓ make a module ↓ separate program responsibilities ↓ make the structure reusable ↓ make a templateEach time, we notice something we are doing repeatedly.
Then we give it a place.
That is one of the ways programs grow without becoming a pile of repeated code.
Try It# Go back to the Raylib exercises you have written so far.
This time, don’t treat each exercise as a separate program that happens to work.
Treat them as a collection of programs and look for things that can be reused.
For each exercise:
Make a fresh copy of raylib_template. Put the code specific to that exercise into sketch.js. Keep main.js unchanged. Look for calculations or functions that are useful in more than one exercise. Move those functions into appropriate modules. Use require() to use those modules from your sketch. You have already seen one example of this with the centering calculation.
Now look for other common mathematics.
For example, you may find calculations involving:
distances coordinates offsets sizes angles movement Create a small library for the mathematics that is common across your exercises.
You might end up with something like:
raylib_template/ ├── main.js ├── sketch.js └── math.jsThe exact functions in math.js are up to you.
The important thing is that you should not have the same useful calculation copied into several different programs.
Instead:
Exercise 1 ──┐ Exercise 2 ──┼──→ math.js Exercise 3 ──┤ Exercise 4 ──┘You are now doing something programmers do all the time:
taking code that works and reorganizing it so that it can be reused.
When you are finished, look at all your exercises again.
Ask yourself:
If I started another Raylib exercise tomorrow, what code would I want to copy?
That code probably belongs in the template or in one of your libraries.
And ask:
What code is specific to this particular exercise?
That code belongs in sketch.js.
The goal is not to create as many files as possible.
The goal is to put each piece of code in a place where it makes sense and can be reused when it should be.

title: Intro to Git/GitHub
content:
So far, whatever the raylib code you wrote has stored on your computer.
Now think about these situations:
What if your laptop suddenly stops working? What if you want your code reviewed by mentors or peers, may be during the weekend? What if your laptop gets lost or damaged? What if you want to access your code from another computer? What if you are away from your laptop but need to look at your latest code? All of these point to the same problem: your code lives in exactly one place.
So we need another copy of it, somewhere other than your laptop.
That other copy is commonly called a:
remote repository
For now, don’t worry about how it is connected.
Just think:
Code on your computer │ │ ▼ Stored on the internetA remote repository is a version of a software project stored on the internet.
GitHub is a service that helps to store our code on the internet.
But wait.
Before we can send anything to the internet, that remote repository has to exist somewhere first.
So the first question is:
How do we create a repository on GitHub?
gh# One way is to open GitHub in your browser and click through the buttons.
But we are already in the terminal. Why leave it?
There is a command available on your machine:
ghgh is GitHub’s official command line tool.
Think of it as:
GitHub │ │ from your terminal ▼ ghgh talks to GitHub for you, without leaving the terminal.
Step 1: Check that gh is available# Run:
gh --versionYou should see something like:
gh version 2.99.0 (2026-09-01) https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/tag/v2.99.0If you see that, gh is installed on your machine.
It’s okay if the version number is different. The important thing is that you see a version number.
Step 2: Check that you are already logged in# Creating a repository means creating it under your GitHub account.
So GitHub needs to know who you are.
This has already been set up for you on your machine. Let’s just confirm it.
Run:
gh auth statusYou should see something like:
github.com ✓ Logged in to github.com account your-username - Active account: true - Git operations protocol: httpsYou may see some extra lines about GitHub token information. You can ignore those.
If you see ✓ Logged in, you are good. Move on to the next step.
But if you see something like:
You are not logged into any GitHub hosts. To log in, run: gh auth loginThen:
Reach out to mentors.
Step 3: Go to one of your projects# Example:
workspace/raylib_exercises/ program.jsMove into that directory:
cd workspace/raylib_exercises Step 4: Make sure it is a Git repository# Before GitHub can store your code, Git has to be tracking it on your computer.
That’s the job of the other command:
gitgit is the tool that keeps the history of your files — what changed, when it changed, and what the code looked like before.
It does not talk to the internet. It works entirely on your machine.
git → keeps history, on your computer gh → talks to GitHub, on the internetTwo commands, two different jobs.
When you run:
git initGit prepares this directory to be managed as a Git repository, allowing Git to keep track of changes made to the files inside it.
That directory is now called a:
Git repository
So, at a basic level:
Directory + Git's tracking information ↓ Git repositoryFor now:
A Git repository is a directory that Git is managing so it can keep track of its history.
Now you have:
Git repositoryon your computer, but nothing on the GitHub yet.
Step 5: Create the repository on GitHub# Run:
gh repo create raylib_exercises --public --source=. --remote=originThat’s one line, but a lot is happening in it.
Let’s break it down:
gh repo create raylib_exercises ↓ create a repository named "raylib_exercises" on GitHub --public ↓ anyone can see it --source=. ↓ use the repository from your current directory --remote=origin ↓ give the GitHub repository the nickname originOnce you run the command, you will see some output like this:
✓ Created repository charan/raylib_exercises on github.com https://github.com/charan/raylib_exercises ✓ Added remote https://github.com/charan/raylib_exercises.gitWhich means that the repository has been created on GitHub and your computer is now connected to it.
Let’s look at two of them a bit more closely.
--publicRemember one of our original questions?
What if you want your code reviewed by mentors or peers?
A public repository means your mentors and peers can simply open the link and look at your code.
--remote=originThis is the piece that links the two sides together:
Your computer GitHub │ │ └────── origin ────────────┘origin is just a name.
It is the name your computer uses to refer to that repository on GitHub.
Step 6: Open the repository in your browser# To open it in the browser:
gh repo view --web The mental model# Your project now exists in two places.
Your computer GitHub (local) (remote) raylib_exercises/ raylib_exercises hello.js hello.js │ ▲ └──────── origin ───────────────┘The copy on your computer is called local.
The copy on GitHub is called remote.
local → where you write your code remote → where your code is stored and sharedYou work on local. You send your changes to remote.
For now, don’t worry about the specifics and about it’s internals etc.
Just hold on to this:
I write code locally. I send it to the remote, so that others can see it.
gacp# Before we move on, let’s be clear about what we have actually done so far.
We created the remote repository:
gh repo create ↓ a place on GitHub to store this projectThat’s it.
Creating the repository is a one-time job. You will not run gh repo create again for this project.
But your code will keep changing.
You will fix a bug today, add a feature tomorrow, change a colour the day after.
None of those changes reach GitHub on their own.
Create the repository → once Send your changes → again and againSo every time you change your code, you still need a way to say:
“Send my latest changes to the remote repository.”
That’s a different job from creating the repository.
gacp is the command for that job.
gacp is a command which helps us to send our code changes from our computer to the remote repository.
you can use:
gacp "fix greeting" How to use gacp# The basic syntax is:
gacp [message]For example:
gacp "fix greeting" Small example with gacp# Suppose you changed:
function draw() { r.DrawText("Hello, world!", 10, 10, 20, r.RAYWHITE); }to:
function draw() { r.DrawText("Good morning, everyone!", 30, 30, 10, r.BLUE); }you can run:
gacp "fix greeting"This helps you to send your code changes to the remote repository.
For now , don’t worry about what exactly happens when you run this command. Just know that it helps you to send your code changes to the remote repository.
The very first gacp in a project may complain that your branch has no upstream branch. That is normal. Run git push -u origin main once, and gacp will work from then on.
Tired of copying your template?# You built a raylib template:
raylib_template/ ├── main.js ├── sketch.js └── geometry.jsAnd every time you start a new project, you copy it:
cp -R ~/workspace/raylib_template ~/workspace/moving_circleCopy again for the next one.
And again for the one after that.
It works, but look at what it depends on.
Your template exists in exactly one place:
~/workspace/raylib_templateon this laptop.
That’s the same problem we started this whole blog with.
And we already know the answer:
Put it on GitHub.
Then the template is not a directory on one laptop anymore.
Step 1: Put the template on GitHub# Nothing new here. It is exactly what you did for your exercises.
cd ~/workspace/raylib_template git init gh repo create raylib_template --public --source=. --remote=origin gacp "add raylib template" gh repo edit --templateOnly the last line is new.
By default GitHub treats this like any other repository. That one command says something more specific:
This repository is a starting point for other projects.
All of this is a one-time job. You will not run these again for your template.
Step 2: Start a new project from it# Now suppose you want to start moving_circle.
Run these four lines:
Please make sure to replace your-username with your actual GitHub username from the below command.
cd ~/workspace gh repo create moving_circle --template your-username/raylib_template --public --clone cd moving_circle git push -u origin mainLet’s break it down.
The second line is the important one:
gh repo create moving_circle ↓ create a new repository named "moving_circle" on GitHub --template your-username/raylib_template ↓ start it from my template --public ↓ anyone can see it --clone ↓ and bring a copy down to this computerYou only need it once per project.
If it says Everything up-to-date, that is fine too. It just means there was nothing new to send.
Now look:
moving_circle/ ├── main.js ├── sketch.js └── geometry.jsAll three files are there, exactly as in your template.
Open sketch.js and start working.
From here on, it is just:
gacp "draw the circle" Sharing your code# Let’s go back to one of the questions we started with:
What if you want your code reviewed by mentors or peers, may be during the weekend?
We can answer it now.
Your repository on GitHub has an address.
To see it, run:
gh repo view --webThis opens your repository in the browser.
Look at the address bar:
https://github.com/your-username/raylib_exercisesThat is the link.
Send that link to your mentor or your peer, and they can open your code from their own computer.
And that closes the loop we opened at the beginning:
Code only on your laptop │ │ git + gh ▼ Code on GitHub │ │ a link ▼ Your mentors and peers can see it

title: Skeleton
content:
Organizing a Raylib Program# You have now written a few small Raylib programs.
You have probably noticed that even a small program starts to contain several different kinds of code:
code that prepares the window code that changes things code that draws things code that keeps the program running It is useful to give these different responsibilities a little structure.
We are going to use the following skeleton:
function setup() {} function update() {} function draw() {} function loop() { update(); draw(); } function main() { setup(); loop(); } main();This is not a rule imposed by Raylib.
It is a way for us to organize our thinking.
Setup# setup() is where we prepare the program.
For example:
function setup() { r.InitWindow(screenWidth, screenHeight, "Center rectangle"); r.SetTargetFPS(FPS); }The window needs to exist before we can draw into it.
The frame rate needs to be configured before the program starts running.
These are things that happen once.
So they belong in setup().
Notice that setup() does not contain the main loop.
It prepares the world. It does not run the world.
The Loop# The program then enters its loop:
function loop() { while (!r.WindowShouldClose()) { update(); draw(); } }There are two things happening repeatedly:
update(); draw();First, we update our program.
Then, we draw what the program currently looks like.
This distinction is important.
For the moment, our update() function can be completely empty:
function update() {}That might seem unnecessary.
Why have a function that does nothing?
Because we are establishing a structure for the program.
Something will eventually need to change.
Representation and Drawing# Consider the rectangle from the previous exercise.
We have:
const screenWidth = 400; const screenHeight = 400; const rectWidth = 200; const rectHeight = 200;These values are a representation of something in our program.
They describe the rectangle.
The drawing code takes that representation and turns it into pixels:
function draw() { const rectX = calcOffset(screenWidth, rectWidth); const rectY = calcOffset(screenHeight, rectHeight); r.BeginDrawing(); r.ClearBackground(r.BLACK); r.DrawRectangle(rectX, rectY, rectWidth, rectHeight, r.WHITE); r.EndDrawing(); }The rectangle’s width and height are part of the state of our program.
The drawing function looks at that state and asks:
Given what the program currently knows, what should I put on the screen?
This is one of the ideas we want to keep developing.
The state of the program and its representation on the screen are not the same thing.
The rectangle can exist as numbers:
width = 200 height = 200without being drawn.
Drawing is something we do with that representation.
Update# Now uncomment these lines from the earlier exercise:
// rectWidth++; // rectHeight--; and change the declarations:
let rectWidth = 200; let rectHeight = 200;We can put the changes into update():
function update() { rectWidth++; rectHeight--; }Now the program has two separate jobs.
update() changes the representation:
function update() { rectWidth++; rectHeight--; }draw() looks at the representation:
function draw() { const rectX = calcOffset(screenWidth, rectWidth); const rectY = calcOffset(screenHeight, rectHeight); r.BeginDrawing(); r.ClearBackground(r.BLACK); r.DrawRectangle(rectX, rectY, rectWidth, rectHeight, r.WHITE); r.EndDrawing(); }The loop connects the two:
while (!r.WindowShouldClose()) { update(); draw(); }Something changes.
Then we show the result of that change.
Then it changes again.
Then we show the new result.
And so on.
This is the basic shape of a great many programs that deal with things changing over time.
Why Keep Them Separate?# Imagine putting everything into draw():
function draw() { rectWidth++; rectHeight--; // draw... }It might work.
But now the function that is supposed to describe what the program looks like is also responsible for changing what the program is.
That makes it harder to reason about.
Instead, we can ask two different questions:
Update:
What has changed?
Draw:
Given the current state, what should be displayed?
These are different questions.
Keeping them separate gives each function a smaller responsibility.
As our programs become more complicated, this distinction becomes increasingly useful.
Functions and Global Variables# There is another thing worth noticing in our draw() function.
It uses these variables:
screenWidth; screenHeight; rectWidth; rectHeight;without receiving them as arguments.
For example, we could have written:
function draw(width, height) { // ... }and passed everything the function needs to it.
In general, this is a good direction for functions.
A function is easier to understand when you can look at its arguments and know what information it needs.
For example:
function calcOffset(x1, x2) { return (x1 - x2) / 2; }You do not need to know anything else about the program to understand this function.
Give it two numbers.
It gives you a number back.
That is a useful property.
An Exception for Now# Our draw() function is different.
It is deliberately using the variables outside itself:
function draw() { const rectX = calcOffset(screenWidth, rectWidth); const rectY = calcOffset(screenHeight, rectHeight); // ... }We are allowing this for now because it makes the structure of these early Raylib programs easier to see.
The program’s state is sitting outside the functions, and draw() is reading that state.
This is an exception to an idea we will be developing.
Eventually, we will work toward programs where our functions do not quietly depend on global variables.
We will have to think carefully about what information a function needs and how that information gets to it.
That is a problem worth solving.
For now, do not solve it.
Notice it.
A Skeleton for Our Programs# For the programs we are writing now, think of this as our basic skeleton:
function setup() { // prepare things } function update() { // change the state } function draw() { // display the current state } function loop() { while (!r.WindowShouldClose()) { update(); draw(); } } function main() { setup(); loop(); } main();There is a useful rhythm here:
setup ↓ update → draw ↑ ↓ └──────┘setup() happens once.
update() and draw() happen repeatedly.
The update changes the representation.
The draw observes that representation.
This gives us a place to put new ideas as our programs become more interesting.
Separating the Program# There is one more change we will eventually make.
Right now, everything is sitting in one file:
program.jsThat is convenient while our programs are small.
It will not remain convenient forever.
Eventually, we will separate the code responsible for our program’s setup, update, and draw from the code responsible for running it.
The exact arrangement is something we will discover as the programs grow.
For now, pay attention to the boundaries we have created.
We have separated:
preparation updating drawing looping Those boundaries are more important than the files they happen to live in.
The files will come later.
Keep Experimenting# Take all of your existing programs and reorganize it using this skeleton.
Do not add new behaviour.
Just move the existing code into setup(), update(), and draw().
Then ask yourself:
What information does each function need? Which values represent the state of the program? Which code changes those values? Which code only reads them? Which functions are depending on variables they did not receive as arguments? Is each function doing one clear job? You are not trying to make the program clever.
You are trying to make its structure easier to see.
That is a useful habit to develop as programs get larger.

title: Simple exercises
content:
First Exercises# You now have a working Raylib program.
You have seen how a Raylib program is structured, and you have used functions such as r.DrawRectangle.
Now it is time to start solving some small problems.
For these exercises, create a directory called:
workspace/raylib_exercises/Each exercise should be its own program.
Use these filenames:
01_center_rectangle.js 02_center_rectangle_in_rectangle.js 03_scale_and_center.js 04_closer_target.jsWrite the Raylib program yourself for each exercise. You should not need to copy the program from the previous post.
Exercise 1: Center a Rectangle# Create a window and draw a rectangle.
Give the rectangle a width and a height.
Your task is to make the rectangle appear exactly in the centre of the window.
Think carefully about what “centre” means.
What do you know about the window?
What do you know about the rectangle?
Where should the rectangle begin?
Try changing the width and height of the rectangle.
Try changing the dimensions of the window.
Does your program still centre the rectangle?
Now write a function that performs the calculation needed to position the rectangle.
What should this function receive?
What should it return?
Can the same function be used to determine both the horizontal and vertical position?
Exercise 2: Center a Rectangle Inside Another Rectangle# Create two rectangles.
Give them different colours.
One rectangle should be larger than the other.
Your task is to place the smaller rectangle exactly in the centre of the larger rectangle.
The larger rectangle does not have to be centred in the window.
Try moving it around.
Try changing its width and height.
Try changing the dimensions of the smaller rectangle.
Does the smaller rectangle remain centred?
Look at the function you wrote for the previous exercise.
Can you use it here?
Exercise 3: Scale and Center# Create an outer rectangle.
This time, don’t specify the dimensions of the inner rectangle directly.
Instead, specify how large the inner rectangle should be relative to the outer rectangle.
For example:
width = 0.8 height = 0.8This should mean that the inner rectangle is 80% as wide and 80% as tall as the outer rectangle.
Calculate the dimensions of the inner rectangle and place it in the centre of the outer rectangle.
Try different values.
What happens at 0.5?
What happens at 0.25?
What happens at 1?
What happens at a value greater than 1?
What parts of this problem are different from the previous exercise?
What parts are exactly the same?
Exercise 4: Find the Closer Target# Draw a circle to represent a source.
Then draw two targets at different positions.
The source and both targets should be visible on the screen.
Your task is to determine which target is closer to the source.
Draw a line from the source to the closer target.
You may want to look back at the r.DrawLine function from the previous post.
How can you determine the distance between two points?
What information do you need about each point?
What happens if you move the source?
What happens if you move either target?
Does your program continue to choose the correct target?
Try several different arrangements of the three points.
What happens when the two targets are the same distance from the source?
Exercise 5: Intersecting Circles# Create two circles at different positions and with different radii.
Your task is to determine whether the two circles intersect.
If the circles intersect, colour both circles red. If the circles do not intersect, colour both circles black. Try different positions for the circles. Try different radii. Try cases where the circles are just touching. Try cases where one circle is completely inside the other. What information about the two circles do you need in order to determine whether they intersect?
Can you express the test for intersection as a function?
What should the function receive?
What should it return?
Try changing the positions and radii after your function is working. Does it continue to give the correct result? (step-12.github.io)
Keep experimenting# These programs are deliberately small.
Don’t rush through them.
Change the numbers.
Move things around.
Try values you did not expect to work.
But also look carefully at the structure of your programs.
As you write more functions, ask yourself:
Does this function do one thing?
Does its name tell me what it does?
Does it receive the information it needs as arguments?
Does it return a useful value rather than changing something somewhere else?
Am I repeating a calculation that could belong in a function?
If I change something in one place, will I have to change it in several other places?
Good programs are not just programs that produce the right answer.
The way we organise the computation matters too.
For now, don’t worry about finding the “perfect” structure.
Write the program.
Get it working.
Then look at it again.
Can you make the functions clearer?
Can you make them easier to reuse?
Can you make the next person reading the program understand what each function is responsible for?
These are questions we will keep returning to.

title: Raylib anatomy
content:
The anatomy of a Raylib program# In the previous post, we saw that Raylib is a library that gives our JavaScript programs a collection of functions for working with graphics.
We are now going to look at a complete Raylib program.
Don’t worry if you don’t understand everything in it yet.
In fact, you shouldn’t.
Read through it once and see if you can recognize anything.
const r = require("raylib"); r.InitWindow(800, 400, "Raylib"); r.SetTargetFPS(60); while (!r.WindowShouldClose()) { r.BeginDrawing(); r.ClearBackground(r.BLACK); r.DrawRectangle(100, 50, 600, 300, r.WHITE); r.EndDrawing(); } r.CloseWindow();There are quite a few things happening here.
Let’s take the program apart.
Getting Raylib# The first line is:
const r = require("raylib");We saw this in the previous post.
We are asking Node.js to give us the Raylib library.
We store what we get in a variable called r.
Why r?
There is nothing particularly special about that name. We could have called it something else.
const raylib = require("raylib");would also work.
For now, think of r as our way of accessing the Raylib toolbox.
So when we write:
r.DrawRectangle(...)we are asking Raylib to perform an operation for us.
We will come back to exactly what require is doing later.
For now, there is something more interesting to understand.
Creating a window# The next line is:
r.InitWindow(800, 400, "Raylib");We are calling a Raylib function called InitWindow.
It creates the window in which our graphics will appear.
Look at the arguments.
800 400 "Raylib"Can you guess what they mean?
The first two are the width and height of the window.
So we are asking for a window that is:
800 pixels wide 400 pixels highThe third argument is the title of the window.
Try changing it.
What happens if you write:
r.InitWindow(800, 400, "My first graphics program");You have already encountered function arguments.
This is no different.
Raylib has simply given us a function that does something useful.
A coordinate system# Remember the coordinate system we saw in the previous post.
The top-left corner of the window is:
(0, 0)The x coordinate increases as we move to the right.
The y coordinate increases as we move down.
So where would this point be?
(100, 50)And this one?
(600, 300)Keep those coordinates in mind.
We are going to use them shortly.
How quickly should we draw?# The next line is:
r.SetTargetFPS(60);FPS means frames per second.
A graphical program produces a sequence of images called frames.
If we produce 60 frames every second, we are producing roughly:
60 frames --------- 1 secondSo this line tells Raylib that we would like the program to run at 60 frames per second.
Why would we want to produce the same image 60 times every second?
That’s a good question.
We will get to the answer.
For now, just remember that our graphical program is going to keep producing frames.
The part that keeps the program running# Now we come to something new.
You can see this:
while (!r.WindowShouldClose()) {You don’t need to understand this line yet.
There are some JavaScript ideas in here that we haven’t properly introduced.
We will learn about while loops later.
For now, all you need to know is this:
This is the part of the program that keeps the drawing process going.
Everything inside the { and } belongs to this repeating part of the program.
So this:
while (...) { // things here }is telling the program that the things inside it should happen repeatedly.
There is also a Raylib function here:
r.WindowShouldClose();You can probably guess what it is asking.
It asks Raylib whether the window should close.
For now, don’t worry about exactly how the while works or how the answer from WindowShouldClose() is used.
We will come back to that when we properly learn loops.
What matters today is that the program needs some way of saying:
Keep producing frames until the window is closed.
Beginning a frame# Inside that repeating part of the program, we have:
r.BeginDrawing();We are beginning to construct one frame.
Think of everything between:
r.BeginDrawing();and:
r.EndDrawing();as the work involved in producing one image.
What should that image look like?
That’s what we are about to describe.
Clearing the screen# The first thing we do is:
r.ClearBackground(r.BLACK);This clears the background and makes it black.
Why do this every frame?
Think about a normal piece of paper.
If you draw a rectangle on paper, it stays there.
If you draw another rectangle, the first rectangle doesn’t disappear.
A screen is different.
We are going to keep describing what the screen should look like right now.
So at the beginning of each frame, we clear what was there before.
Then we draw what we want to see.
You might find it interesting to remove this line and see what happens.
Don’t worry if you don’t yet understand exactly why it happens.
Just observe it.
Drawing the rectangle# Now we get to something familiar:
r.DrawRectangle(100, 50, 600, 300, r.WHITE);This is a function call.
Raylib has provided a function called DrawRectangle.
We give it five arguments.
Can you guess what they are?
Look at the rectangle we are drawing.
x → 100 y → 50 width → 600 height → 300 color → WHITESo the rectangle begins at:
(100, 50)and has a width of 600 and a height of 300.
Its colour is white.
We have already encountered everything necessary to understand the idea of this function call.
We know how to call functions.
We know how arguments work.
We know about numbers.
We know about values.
Raylib is simply providing us with a function that has a visible effect.
Ending the frame# After drawing the rectangle, we have:
r.EndDrawing();We have finished describing this frame.
Raylib can now finish the frame and present it on the screen.
And then something interesting happens.
The program goes back to the repeating part.
It begins another frame.
The whole thing happens again# Let’s look at the important part again:
while (!r.WindowShouldClose()) { r.BeginDrawing(); r.ClearBackground(r.BLACK); r.DrawRectangle(100, 50, 600, 300, r.WHITE); r.EndDrawing(); }The first time around, we produce something like:
FRAME 1 black background white rectangleThen another frame is produced:
FRAME 2 black background white rectangleThen another:
FRAME 3 black background white rectangleAnd another.
And another.
At 60 frames per second, this happens many times every second.
But the rectangle doesn’t appear to move.
Why?
Because we are drawing it in exactly the same place every time.
We keep telling Raylib:
Draw a white rectangle at (100, 50).
So that’s what we see.
Now imagine that the position of the rectangle changed between one frame and the next.
What might happen?
We will explore that later.
Closing the window# There is one line left:
r.CloseWindow();Notice where it is.
It is outside the repeating part of the program.
That means it happens after we are finished producing frames.
When you close the window, Raylib knows that it is time for the repeating part of the program to finish.
The program then reaches:
r.CloseWindow();and Raylib can clean up the window before our program finishes.
You don’t need to understand the exact mechanics of how this works yet.
We will learn about the JavaScript mechanisms involved when we study loops.
The shape of a Raylib program# We can now look at the whole program in a different way.
Get Raylib ↓ Create a window ↓ Set the frame rate ↓ ┌───────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Begin a frame │ │ ↓ │ │ Clear the screen │ │ ↓ │ │ Draw things │ │ ↓ │ │ End the frame │ │ ↓ │ │ Repeat │ │ │ └───────────────────────────┘ ↓ Close the windowThis is the basic shape of the Raylib programs we will be writing.
There is a part that happens once at the beginning.
There is a part that happens repeatedly.
And there is a part that happens when we are finished.
The repeating part is particularly important.
It is what allows our program to produce a sequence of frames rather than just one picture.
There is still a lot we don’t know# There are things in this program that we have deliberately not explained.
For example:
What exactly does require do? What is r really? What exactly does while mean? How does the program know when to repeat? How does Raylib know when the window has been closed? How does Raylib create a window? How does DrawRectangle turn five values into pixels? What happens inside BeginDrawing() and EndDrawing()? How does Raylib keep track of 60 frames per second? Those are all interesting questions.
We will answer some of them later.
For now, you have something more useful.
You have a working program.
And you have a mental model of its shape.
You don’t need to understand every line yet.
Now change something# Before moving on, run the program yourself.
Then start changing things.
What happens if you change:
r.InitWindow(800, 400, "Raylib");to:
r.InitWindow(400, 400, "Raylib");What happens if you change:
r.DrawRectangle(100, 50, 600, 300, r.WHITE);to:
r.DrawRectangle(200, 100, 100, 100, r.WHITE);What happens if you change the colour?
What happens if you draw a second rectangle?
What happens if you remove ClearBackground()?
Don’t worry about making a useful program yet.
For now, change something, run the program, and look carefully at what happened.
Soon, we’ll start turning these experiments into small programming problems.

title: Intro to Graphics/Raylib
content:
Raylib# So far, most of the programs you have written have produced things like numbers and text.
You might have written:
console.log(2 + 3);and seen:
5Or perhaps you wrote a function that takes some values, performs a computation, and returns another value.
What if the result of our program could be something that we could see?
What if instead of producing:
5our program could produce a rectangle on the screen?
That is where we are going next.
A different kind of output# Imagine that your computer has a large sheet of graph paper in front of it.
The sheet is made up of many tiny points called pixels. We can describe a position on this sheet using two numbers.
We usually call them x and y.
(0, 0) ┌──────────────────────────────→ x │ │ │ │ ↓ yThe top-left corner is (0, 0).
Move to the right and x increases.
Move down and y increases.
So where would (100, 50) be?
And where would (500, 200) be?
You don’t have to draw these points. Just try to imagine them.
Now suppose we wanted to draw a rectangle.
A rectangle needs more information than just a position.
We need to know:
where it starts; how wide it is; how tall it is; what colour it should be. So perhaps we could describe a rectangle like this:
x = 100 y = 50 width = 200 height = 100We have turned something visual into data.
This is an important idea.
Graphics are something that a program can describe.
A rectangle is not mysterious to the computer. It can be described using numbers.
A line can be described using positions.
A circle can be described using a position, a radius, and a colour.
A picture can be described using many such things together.
So how do we get our JavaScript program to actually draw them?
Somebody has already written the code# Think back to functions.
Suppose you need to calculate whether a number is even. You could write the function yourself:
function isEven(number) { return number % 2 === 0; }But what if somebody else had already written a useful function?
You could simply use it.
This happens all the time in programming.
You do not have to write every piece of code yourself.
Other programmers write collections of useful code that we can use in our own programs.
These collections are called libraries.
A library is, broadly speaking, code written by somebody else that we can use in our own programs.
You have already used libraries without necessarily thinking about them as libraries.
Now we are going to use one deliberately.
Raylib# We are going to use a library called Raylib.
Raylib contains functions for doing things with graphics.
For example, it has functions for:
creating a window; drawing rectangles; drawing lines; drawing circles; displaying text; working with the keyboard; working with the mouse; and many other things. Imagine that somebody has spent a great deal of time writing all the difficult code necessary to make a rectangle appear on a screen.
We don’t need to write all of that code ourselves.
Instead, we can call a function they have provided.
The idea should feel familiar.
We know how to call functions:
someFunction(10, 20);Raylib gives us functions that do useful things with graphics.
For example, there is a function called DrawRectangle.
We will eventually be able to write something like:
r.DrawRectangle(100, 50, 200, 100, r.WHITE);What do you think those five values might mean?
Look back at our description of a rectangle.
There is a position.
There is a width and a height.
And there is a colour.
You can probably make a good guess.
That’s enough for now.
We will discover the rest by using it.
Using Raylib from JavaScript# Raylib itself is not a JavaScript library.
We are writing JavaScript programs using Node.js, so we need a way for our JavaScript programs to use Raylib.
We will use node-raylib for this.
Before we can use it, we need to add it to our project.
Open your terminal and move into your JavaScript workspace.
Then install Raylib:
npm install raylibYou may have seen npm before. It is a tool that helps us work with packages of JavaScript code.
When you install a package, you will also see a file called:
package.jsonThis file describes our Node.js project and, among other things, keeps track of the packages that our project uses.
Don’t worry about learning npm or package.json in detail right now.
We have a much more interesting question to answer:
What can we make with Raylib?
A toolbox# For now, think of Raylib as a toolbox.
Our JavaScript program is still our program.
We still have:
const let if while function returnand everything else that we have learned.
Raylib simply gives us some additional tools.
Instead of writing all the code necessary to draw a rectangle ourselves, we can use the tool that Raylib gives us.
Instead of writing all the code necessary to create a window, we can use the tool that Raylib gives us.
