Instead of writing all the code necessary to read a keyboard key, we can eventually use the tool that Raylib gives us.
The programming language has not changed.
We have simply acquired a new collection of things that our program can do.
There is a lot here# If you look at the Raylib documentation, you will find a lot of functions.
There are functions for things we have not talked about yet.
There are concepts we have not learned yet.
There are probably things that will make very little sense to you right now.
That is completely fine.
In fact, you should expect this.
We are going to learn Raylib gradually.
At first, we will only use a handful of functions.
Later, we will discover more.
Some things will remain mysterious until we have learned the programming concepts necessary to understand them.
You do not need to understand everything you see.
You need to understand enough to start experimenting.
A new kind of programming# Up to now, when you wrote a program, you were mostly asking:
What value should this expression produce?
Or:
What should this function return?
We are going to start asking some different questions.
Where should this rectangle be?
What happens if I move it?
What happens if two rectangles overlap?
How could I make a circle move?
How could I make something respond to the keyboard?
How could I make a game?
These are still programming questions.
We will still use variables.
We will still use conditions.
We will still use functions.
We will still use the same JavaScript.
But now our programs will have a world in which those ideas can operate.
That is what makes this interesting.
One last question# There is one thing you should notice.
If a program draws a rectangle, does it draw the rectangle once and then finish?
What would happen if you wanted the rectangle to move?
Would the program have to draw the rectangle again?
And again?
And again?
We will answer that next.
For now, don’t worry about how.
Just keep the question in your head:
How does a program keep drawing things on the screen?

title: JS Recursion
content:
Recursion Assignments# For these assignments, you do not need to learn anything new about JavaScript. Use the things you already know: functions, parameters, return values, strings, numbers, conditionals, and basic operators.
There are three small problems.
1. Nested Parentheses# Write a function that takes a number n and returns a string containing n pairs of nested parentheses.
For example:
5 → "((((()))))"There are five opening parentheses followed by five closing parentheses.
Some more examples:
0 → "" 1 → "()" 2 → "(())" 3 → "((()))" 4 → "(((())))"Your function should work for any non-negative integer n.
For example:
parentheses(3) // "((()))" parentheses(5) // "((((()))))" Think about it# What should the function return when n is 0?
Once you know that, ask yourself:
If I already know how to make n - 1 pairs of parentheses, how could I use that to make n pairs?
Your solution must use recursion.
Make sure your function returns a value and doesn’t simply console.log the value!
2. The Growing and Shrinking Pattern# Write a function that takes a number n and produces a pattern of stars.
For n = 3, the result should be:
* ** *** ** *For n = 4:
* ** *** **** *** ** *For n = 1:
*And for n = 0, the result should be an empty string.
The function should return one string containing newline characters.
For example:
pattern(3) // "*\n**\n***\n**\n*" Make sure your function returns a value and doesn’t simply console.log the value!
3. The Two Spacecraft# You are travelling through a strange region of space where ships do not travel in straight lines.
Instead, they follow fixed routes through a sequence of gates.
There are two routes.
The first route is:
Aurora → Ember → Nebula → Rift → Aurora → ...The second route is:
Ember → Nebula → Rift → Obsidian → Eclipse → Ember → ...Each ship moves one gate forward on every move.
The first ship starts at Aurora.
The second ship starts at Ember.
So at the beginning:
Ship 1: Aurora Ship 2: EmberAfter one move:
Ship 1: Ember Ship 2: NebulaAfter two moves:
Ship 1: Nebula Ship 2: RiftAnd so on.
Eventually, the two ships will be at the same gate at the same time.
Your job is to find how many moves it takes for them to meet.
Your function# Write a function that takes the two starting positions and returns the number of moves until the two ships are at the same gate.
For example, with the routes above:
meet("Aurora", "Ember")should return:
?You must work out the answer.
The function should also work when the starting positions are different.
For example:
meet("Rift", "Obsidian")and
meet("Nebula", "Eclipse")should each produce the correct number of moves.
Important detail# The two ships move at the same time.
A move means that both ships advance by one position.
You are not looking for the first time either ship visits the other’s gate. You are looking for the first time:
ship 1's current gate === ship 2's current gateafter both have made the same number of moves.
The routes# Treat these as cycles. When a ship reaches the end of its route, it goes back to the beginning.
First route:
Aurora → Ember → Nebula → Rift → Aurora → ...Second route:
Ember → Nebula → Rift → Obsidian → Eclipse → Ember → ...Your solution must use recursion. Do not use a for or while loop to repeatedly move the ships.
Recursion — Solutions# In the previous post, you were given three problems to solve using recursion.
There is a useful way to think about all three of them:
Solve a smaller version of the problem, then use that answer to construct the larger answer.
This is the basic pattern we will follow.
For every recursive function, we want to identify two things:
The smallest problem we can solve directly. How to construct a larger problem from a smaller problem. Let’s look at the three problems again.
1. Parentheses# We wanted:
parentheses(0) → "" parentheses(1) → "()" parentheses(2) → "(())" parentheses(3) → "((()))" parentheses(4) → "(((())))"Look closely at these answers.
For parentheses(2):
(())We can see it as three pieces:
( + () + )But () is exactly:
parentheses(1)So:
parentheses(2) = "(" + parentheses(1) + ")"Now look at parentheses(3):
((()))Again, we can decompose it:
( + (()) + )And (()) is:
parentheses(2)So:
parentheses(3) = "(" + parentheses(2) + ")"The same thing works for every value of n.
parentheses(n) = "(" + parentheses(n - 1) + ")"We have decomposed the problem.
Now we need to compose the answer.
function parentheses(n) { return n <= 0 ? "" : "(" + parentheses(n - 1) + ")"; }There is also a very important question here:
When should we stop?
Eventually we reach:
parentheses(0)There is nothing inside the parentheses, so the answer is simply:
""That is our base case.
We can now trace the function:
parentheses(3) "(" + parentheses(2) + ")" "(" + "(" + parentheses(1) + ")" + ")" "(" + "(" + "(" + parentheses(0) + ")" + ")" + ")" "(" + "(" + "(" + "" + ")" + ")" + ")" "((()))"Notice what happened.
We did not tell the computer how to construct all three pairs at once.
We told it:
To make n pairs, make one pair around the answer for n - 1.
That is decomposition followed by composition.
2. The Pattern# Our second problem was to produce:
* ** *** ** *for n = 3.
There are several ways to think about this problem.
Let’s start by looking at just the individual lines.
We can write a small function that produces a line of stars:
function stars(n) { return n <= 0 ? "" : "*" + stars(n - 1); }Again, notice the decomposition.
For example:
stars(3) = "*" + stars(2) = "*" + "*" + stars(1) = "*" + "*" + "*" + stars(0) = "***"So now we have a useful building block.
We can think of our pattern as three pieces:
* ** *** ** *The middle line is the largest line.
Everything before it grows toward that line, and everything after it shrinks away from it.
One way to express that directly is:
function pattern(n, i) { const line = stars(i); if (i >= n) return line; return line + "\n" + pattern(n, i + 1) + "\n" + line; }We start with:
pattern(5, 1)The i parameter tells us which line we are currently constructing.
For example:
pattern(5, 1)can be decomposed into:
stars(1) + pattern(5, 2) + stars(1)Then pattern(5, 2) becomes:
stars(2) + pattern(5, 3) + stars(2)And so on.
Eventually:
pattern(5, 5)is simply:
*****The recursion then returns, composing the complete answer as it goes.
A useful helper# There is something slightly awkward about this version.
We keep writing:
line + "\n" + something + "\n" + lineWe can extract that operation into its own function:
function join(a, b, c) { const NEWLINE = "\n"; return a + NEWLINE + b + NEWLINE + c; }Now our recursive function becomes:
function pattern(n, i) { const line = stars(i); if (i >= n) return line; return join(line, pattern(n, i + 1), line); }The recursive idea is now easier to see:
Put the current line above and below the smaller pattern.
The join function is not doing anything fundamentally new. It merely gives a name to an operation we were already performing.
That is often a useful thing to do when programming.
If you see the same piece of logic appearing repeatedly, you can give that logic a name.
Another way to solve the pattern# There is another interesting decomposition.
Instead of keeping track of which line we are on, we can make the string of stars itself part of the recursive state.
function pattern(n, stars) { if (n <= 1) return stars; return stars + "\n" + pattern(n - 1, stars + "*") + "\n" + stars; }We would start with:
pattern(5, "*")Let’s decompose this.
The first call is:
pattern(5, "*")which becomes:
"*" + pattern(4, "**") + "*"Then:
pattern(4, "**")becomes:
"**" + pattern(3, "***") + "**"And eventually:
pattern(1, "*****")returns:
"*****"The recursion then composes the answer on the way back out.
Comparing the two# The two solutions are solving the same problem, but they represent the problem differently.
The first version says:
pattern(n, i)where i means:
“Which line am I currently working on?”
The second says:
pattern(n, stars)where stars means:
“What should the current line look like?”
Neither representation is inherently correct or incorrect.
The first separates two ideas:
How many lines? Which line?and uses stars() to construct the line.
The second carries the already-constructed line through the recursion.
This gives us a useful programming lesson:
The way you represent the state of a problem can change the shape of the solution.
The second version is shorter and has fewer moving parts. The first version separates the two concerns more explicitly and gives us a reusable stars() function.
There is a tradeoff between simplicity of the final code and how explicitly the different pieces of the problem are represented.
3. The Two Spacecraft# Our final problem involved two spacecraft travelling around different routes.
The first route was:
Aurora → Ember → Nebula → Rift → Aurora → ...The second route was:
Ember → Nebula → Rift → Obsidian → Eclipse → Ember → ...We want to know how many moves it takes until both spacecraft are at the same gate.
The key observation is surprisingly simple.
Suppose the ships are currently here:
Ship 1: Ember Ship 2: RiftAfter one move, they will be here:
Ship 1: Nebula Ship 2: ObsidianSo the larger problem can be decomposed into:
Move both ships once, then solve the same problem again.
That gives us:
meet(Ember, Rift) = 1 + meet(Nebula, Obsidian)And if they are already at the same gate:
meet(Nebula, Nebula)the answer is simply:
0That gives us the recursive structure:
function meet(gate1, gate2) { return gate1 === gate2 ? 0 : 1 + meet( nextGateOnRoute1(gate1), nextGateOnRoute2(gate2) ); }The decomposition is:
meet(current positions) ↓ move both ships ↓ meet(new positions)The composition is:
1 + answer for the smaller problemAgain:
Solve the smaller problem, then use its answer to solve the larger problem.
Making the composition easier to read# The code above works, but the recursive call is a little difficult to read:
1 + meet( nextGateOnRoute1(gate1), nextGateOnRoute2(gate2) )We can make the structure more obvious by giving another operation a name.
Suppose we want a function that combines three pieces of text with newlines:
function join(a, b, c) { return a + "\n" + b + "\n" + c; }Then:
join("hello", "world", "!")produces:
hello world !The function is useful because it hides an uninteresting detail.
Instead of repeatedly writing:
a + "\n" + b + "\n" + cwe can simply write:
join(a, b, c)The same idea appeared in the second problem.
Extracting a function# Suppose we initially wrote our pattern like this:
return line + "\n" + pattern(n, i + 1) + "\n" + line;We can look at that and notice:
a + "\n" + b + "\n" + cis an operation in its own right.
So we extract it:
function join(a, b, c) { return a + "\n" + b + "\n" + c; }and now write:
return join(line, pattern(n, i + 1), line);This is called composition.
We are building a larger operation out of smaller operations.
Can join be made smaller?# Look at our three-argument version:
function join(a, b, c) { return a + "\n" + b + "\n" + c; }There is another way to see this.
What does join(a, b, c) really do?
It joins a and b, and then joins that result with c.
So perhaps join itself can be defined using a smaller join.
Let’s make join take only two arguments:
function join(a, b) { return a + "\n" + b; }Now we can compose it:
join(join(a, b), c)The inner call:
join(a, b)produces:
a bThen the outer call:
join(join(a, b), c)produces:
a b cSo our original three-argument operation:
join(a, b, c)can instead be expressed as:
join(join(a, b), c)This is a small example of an important idea:
Large operations can be constructed by composing smaller operations.
We have seen the same idea three times now.
For parentheses:
"(" + parentheses(n - 1) + ")"For the pattern:
join(line, smallerPattern, line)And for joining:
join(join(a, b), c) Putting the ideas together# Recursion can initially feel like a strange trick:
“A function calls itself.”
But that is not really the interesting part.
The interesting question is:
What smaller version of this problem can I solve?
For the parentheses problem:
parentheses(n) ↓ parentheses(n - 1)For the pattern:
pattern(n) ↓ smaller patternFor the spacecraft:
meet(current positions) ↓ meet(after one move)Then ask:
How do I use the smaller answer to construct the larger answer?
That is the second half of recursion.
You are repeatedly doing two things:
DECOMPOSE ↓ find a smaller problem COMPOSE ↓ use its answer to construct the current answerOnce you start seeing problems this way, recursion becomes less mysterious.
It becomes a way of describing a problem in terms of itself, but smaller.

title: More about functions
content:
Function calls inside function calls# So far, you have seen function calls like this:
double(5)When you see this, you know that double(5) is an expression. The function runs, and eventually the expression produces a value.
Let’s make the expression a little more interesting.
Suppose we have:
function double(number) { return number * 2; } function addOne(number) { return number + 1; }Now consider:
addOne(double(5))Don’t run it yet.
What value should addOne receive?
Think about what has to happen first.
addOne needs an argument. In this case, its argument is:
double(5)So JavaScript first needs to find out what double(5) produces.
double(5) ↓ 10 ↓ addOne(10) ↓ 11So:
addOne(double(5))produces:
11Try it in the REPL.
Now try this:
double(addOne(5))Is the answer still 11?
No.
This time:
addOne(5) ↓ 6 ↓ double(6) ↓ 12The order in which the functions are written matters.
Look inside first# You have already learned to think about expressions as trees.
Consider:
addOne(double(5))There is an outer function call:
addOne | double | 5The addOne call cannot be completed until its argument is known.
That means the inner expression:
double(5)has to be evaluated first.
Then its result becomes the argument to addOne.
Let’s make the expression slightly bigger:
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }Now:
add(double(5), addOne(5))There are two function calls inside the arguments to add.
What does add eventually receive?
Work it out before running it.
double(5) → 10 addOne(5) → 6 add(10, 6) → 16So the whole expression produces:
16Notice something important.
add could not finish until both of its arguments had been evaluated.
You can think of the expression tree like this:
add / \ double addOne | | 5 5The smaller expressions have to produce their values before the larger expression can be completed.
Try these in the REPL:
add(double(3), addOne(7))and:
addOne(double(addOne(3)))Don’t just calculate the final answer.
Ask yourself:
Which function call has to happen first?
Then:
What value does it produce?
Then:
Where does that value go?
This is going to become increasingly important.
What is executing right now?# Consider this:
function double(number) { return number * 2; } function addOne(number) { return number + 1; } console.log(addOne(double(5)));Let’s slow this down.
The first thing that needs to happen is:
double(5)While double is running, has addOne run yet?
No.
addOne is waiting.
In fact, the whole expression is waiting for double(5) to produce a value.
You can imagine the situation like this:
addOne(double(5)) ↑ waitingThen double(5) finishes:
double(5) → 10Now the expression has effectively become:
addOne(10)So addOne can run:
addOne(10) → 11And finally:
console.log(11)runs.
There is a useful way to describe this:
A function call can be waiting for another function call to finish.
Let’s make this visible.
While double(5) is running, imagine that we have:
addOne(double(5))and we are currently inside:
double(5)When double returns 10, we go back to where we were waiting.
Then we continue with:
addOne(10)This happens every time one function calls another.
But there is a problem.
What if the calls become deeper?
Consider:
f(g(h(x)))What is running?
What is waiting?
And where do we go when a function returns?
We need a better model.
The call stack# Let’s look at a small example again:
function double(number) { return number * 2; } function addOne(number) { return number + 1; } console.log(addOne(double(5)));We know that double(5) happens first.
Imagine that JavaScript keeps track of the calls that are currently active.
When double(5) begins, we can imagine this:
double(5)Then double returns.
It is finished, so it disappears:
Now addOne(10) begins:
addOne(10)Then that finishes too.
This collection of currently active calls is called the call stack.
The word stack is useful here because calls are added and removed in a particular order.
A new call goes on top.
When a call finishes, the call on top is removed.
Let’s look at a slightly deeper example.
function a(number) { return b(number); } function b(number) { return c(number); } function c(number) { return number + 1; } console.log(a(5));Don’t run it yet.
What happens when we call:
a(5)a begins running.
a(5)Then a calls b(5).
Now both calls are active:
b(5) a(5)b is on top because it is the function currently executing.
Then b calls c(5):
c(5) b(5) a(5)Now c returns:
c(5) → 6So c disappears:
b(5) a(5)b can now continue. It receives the value 6 from c.
Then b returns:
b(5) → 6Now:
a(5)is all that remains.
Finally, a returns:
a(5) → 6And the call stack is empty again.
The important thing to notice is that calls don’t all run at once.
At any particular moment, there is a function call that is currently executing, while other calls are waiting underneath it.
You can draw the stack yourself when tracing a program.
For example:
function f(number) { return g(number + 1); } function g(number) { return h(number * 2); } function h(number) { return number - 3; } console.log(f(4));Before you run it, draw the call stack as it changes.
Ask yourself:
Which function is executing at this point?
What is waiting for it?
What happens when it returns?
This is exactly where your expression-tree model and the call-stack model work together.
The expression tree helps you see what needs to be evaluated.
The call stack helps you see which calls are currently active and which calls are waiting.
When a function calls itself# There is one more kind of function call we need to understand.
You already know this idea from mathematics.
For example:
factorial(5) = 5 × factorial(4) factorial(4) = 4 × factorial(3) factorial(3) = 3 × factorial(2) factorial(2) = 2 × factorial(1) factorial(1) = 1You have already seen that a mathematical definition can describe a problem in terms of a smaller version of the same problem.
We can write the same idea in JavaScript:
function factorial(number) { if (number === 1) { return 1; } return number * factorial(number - 1); }Look carefully at this line:
return number * factorial(number - 1);What happens when we call:
factorial(5)Don’t run it yet.
The function reaches:
factorial(5 - 1)which is:
factorial(4)So now another call to factorial begins.
The call stack looks like:
factorial(4) factorial(5)Then factorial(4) calls:
factorial(3)So:
factorial(3) factorial(4) factorial(5)Then:
factorial(2) factorial(3) factorial(4) factorial(5)Then:
factorial(1) factorial(2) factorial(3) factorial(4) factorial(5)Now something different happens.
factorial(1) reaches:
if (number === 1) { return 1; }It returns.
So factorial(1) disappears from the stack.
But factorial(2) has not finished.
It was waiting for the result of:
factorial(1)Now that result is available:
factorial(1) → 1So factorial(2) can finish:
2 × 1 → 2Then:
factorial(3) → 3 × 2 → 6Then:
factorial(4) → 4 × 6 → 24And finally:
factorial(5) → 5 × 24 → 120The calls grew downwards:
factorial(5) factorial(4) factorial(3) factorial(2) factorial(1)Then they returned upwards:
factorial(1) → 1 factorial(2) → 2 factorial(3) → 6 factorial(4) → 24 factorial(5) → 120There is nothing special about the call stack here.
This is important.
Recursion does not create a new kind of function call.
It is still just a function call.
The only unusual thing is that the function calls itself.
A smaller recursive example# Let’s look at one where the output is easier to see.
function countdown(number) { if (number === 0) { return; } console.log(number); countdown(number - 1); }What will this print?
Don’t run it.
Predict:
countdown(3);You should be able to trace:
countdown(3) countdown(2) countdown(1) countdown(0)But notice when the console.log happens.
countdown(3) prints 3 before making the next call.
Then countdown(2) prints 2.
Then countdown(1) prints 1.
So the output is:
3 2 1Now look at the function again.
There is no value being built up and returned here. The observable result comes from:
console.log(number);That is different from our factorial example, where the important result was the value returned by the function.
Let’s write another recursive function:
function sumTo(number) { if (number === 0) { return 0; } return number + sumTo(number - 1); }What does this produce?
sumTo(4)Trace the calls:
sumTo(4) sumTo(3) sumTo(2) sumTo(1) sumTo(0)Now trace the returns:
sumTo(0) → 0 sumTo(1) → 1 + 0 → 1 sumTo(2) → 2 + 1 → 3 sumTo(3) → 3 + 3 → 6 sumTo(4) → 4 + 6 → 10Notice how closely this resembles the factorial example.
The function keeps asking for the answer to a smaller problem.
Eventually it reaches the smallest problem it knows how to answer directly.
That is why the condition:
if (number === 0)is so important.
Without it, the calls would keep going.
One more thing about recursion# You might reasonably ask:
Why not just write five lines and calculate the answer?
For example, why not calculate:
4 + 3 + 2 + 1directly?
Sometimes you should.
Recursion is not something you should use merely because you can.
It becomes useful when a problem naturally has this shape:
To solve this problem, solve a smaller version of the same problem.
Mathematical recursion is a good example because the definition itself has that structure.
You already know this way of thinking from mathematics. JavaScript is simply giving you a way to execute those definitions.
Trace before you run# Let’s finish with something more difficult.
Consider:
function f(number) { if (number === 0) { console.log("zero"); return 0; } console.log("before", number); const result = f(number - 1); console.log("after", number); return result + number; } console.log(f(3));Don’t run it.
Take your time.
First, what is the first thing f(3) does?
It prints:
before 3Then it calls:
f(2)So we get:
before 3 before 2Then:
f(1)Then:
before 3 before 2 before 1Then f(0).
That call prints:
zeroand returns 0.
But are we finished?
No.
Look at the line after the recursive call:
console.log("after", number);Remember: the earlier calls were waiting.
So after f(0) returns, f(1) continues.
Then f(2) continues.
Then f(3) continues.
The complete output is:
before 3 before 2 before 1 zero after 1 after 2 after 3 6The returned value is 6.
This is a good example to trace with a call stack.
While f(0) is running, the stack looks roughly like:
f(0) f(1) f(2) f(3)f(0) returns.
Then:
f(1) f(2) f(3)f(1) prints "after", 1 and returns.
Then:
f(2) f(3)And so on.
The important thing is that the function calls do not disappear just because they are waiting.
They remain on the stack.
They are waiting for the call above them to return.
Exercises# For each exercise, create a separate JavaScript file.
Do not run the program until you have made a prediction.
1. Nested calls# Write:
function double(number) { return number * 2; } function addOne(number) { return number + 1; }Then determine the value of:
addOne(double(10))and:
double(addOne(10))Write your predicted answers as comments before running the program.
2. A function as an argument# Write an add function that takes two numbers and returns their sum.
Then determine the result of:
add(double(4), addOne(4))Trace each inner call before calculating the final result.
3. Several levels deep# Write three functions:
f g hwhere f calls g, and g calls h.
Call:
f(5)Draw the call stack as the program runs.
Then draw it again as the functions return.
4. Draw the stack# Without running this program, draw the call stack at its deepest point:
function a(number) { return b(number); } function b(number) { return c(number); } function c(number) { return d(number); } function d(number) { return number + 1; } console.log(a(5));Then determine the final value.
5. Recursive mathematics# Write a recursive JavaScript function for a mathematical recursive definition you already know.
For example, you could implement factorial.
Before running it, write down the sequence of calls for:
factorial(4)6. Trace the returns# For:
function sumTo(number) { if (number === 0) { return 0; } return number + sumTo(number - 1); }Trace:
sumTo(5)Write down every call and every returned value.
7. Predict the output# Do not run this program:
function f(number) { if (number === 0) { console.log("done"); return 0; } console.log("enter", number); const result = f(number - 1); console.log("leave", number); return result + number; } console.log(f(3));Write the exact output, in order.
Then draw the call stack at its deepest point.
Only after you have finished both should you run the program and check your answer.
The mental model# You now have several ways of looking at the same program.
When you see an expression such as:
add(double(5), addOne(5))you can think in terms of an expression tree.
The tree shows you which expressions have to be evaluated to produce the final value.
When those expressions contain function calls, you can think about the call stack.
The stack shows you which function calls are currently active and which calls are waiting.
And when a function calls itself, you can use exactly the same model.
sumTo(4)creates a call to sumTo(3).
That creates a call to sumTo(2).
That creates a call to sumTo(1).
And so on.
There is no special machinery you need to imagine.
It is still:
call a function → wait for it to return → continue.
The difference is simply that the function happens to call itself.
When you can look at a program and answer:
What is being evaluated?
Which function is executing?
What is waiting?
What value is this call waiting for?
What happens when this function returns?
you are no longer just reading the syntax of a function call.
You are beginning to see the execution of the program.

title: Functions
content:
You have now started writing JavaScript programs in files.
Until now, you have mostly been asking JavaScript questions in the REPL:
> 10 % 2 === 0 true > 17 % 2 === 0 falseNow you can put those expressions into a program, save the program in a file, and run it.
Today, we are going to look at a problem that appears very quickly when you start writing larger programs:
What do you do when you find yourself writing the same computation again and again?
The problem of repetition# Suppose you want to check whether three numbers are even.
Open a new file called even.js.
You could write:
const number1 = 12; const number2 = 17; const number3 = 24; if (number1 % 2 === 0) { console.log(true); } else { console.log(false); } if (number2 % 2 === 0) { console.log(true); } else { console.log(false); } if (number3 % 2 === 0) { console.log(true); } else { console.log(false); }Run the program.
You should get:
true false trueNow look carefully at the three if statements.
What changes between them?
What stays the same?
The numbers change:
number1; number2; number3;But the actual computation does not change:
number % 2 === 0;We have written the same idea three times.
Imagine that instead of three numbers, you had thirty numbers.
Would you want to write this thirty times?
There is something interesting about this repetition.
The computation:
number % 2 === 0;is useful enough that we would like to give it a name.
Then, instead of writing out the computation every time, perhaps we could say:
“Do the even-number computation here.”
JavaScript gives us a way to do exactly that.
Give the computation a name# Replace the previous program with this:
function isEven(number) { return number % 2 === 0; }Read it carefully.
We have given the computation a name:
isEven;Now try calling it:
console.log(isEven(12)); console.log(isEven(17)); console.log(isEven(24));Run the program.
You should see:
true false trueNotice something important.
We only wrote the computation once:
number % 2 === 0;We can now use it as many times as we want.
Try adding:
console.log(isEven(0)); console.log(isEven(101)); console.log(isEven(200));Before running the program, predict the output.
Then run it.
What happened?# Look at this:
isEven(12);You already know what this looks like.
Earlier, you learned to write:
console.log(12);That is a function call.
Now you have written another function call:
isEven(12);The 12 is the argument to the function.
Look back at the function itself:
function isEven(number) { return number % 2 === 0; }There are several pieces here.
function isEven (number) { ... } │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └── body │ │ └── parameter │ └── function name └── tells JavaScript we are defining a functionThe name number is a parameter.
It is the name we use for the value supplied when the function is called.
So when you write:
isEven(12);you can think of the function as performing its computation with number representing 12.
When you write:
isEven(17);number represents 17 instead.
Try this in the REPL:
function isEven(number) { return number % 2 === 0; }Then:
isEven(12);and:
isEven(13);Try several different numbers.
You have now taken a computation and given it a name.
That is already useful.
But there is something more interesting happening here.
What if we need more than one value?# So far, our function has taken one value:
function isEven(number) { return number % 2 === 0; }What if the computation needs two values?
Let’s try a simple example.
Suppose we want to add two numbers.
We could write:
function add(first, second) { return first + second; }Now look at the function definition:
function add(first, second) {There are two parameters:
first secondWhen we call the function, we can give it two arguments:
add(10, 20);What do you think this produces?
Try it in the REPL.
You should get:
30The first argument goes to the first parameter:
first → 10and the second argument goes to the second parameter:
second → 20So you can imagine the function’s table looking like this while it is running:
Name Value first 10 second 20 The function then evaluates:
first + second;which gives:
30Try changing the arguments# Predict the result of each of these before running them:
add(5, 7);add(100, 25);add(10, -3);The order matters.
What do you think this produces?
add(10, 20);What about:
add(20, 10);For add, the answer happens to be the same.
Let’s use a function where the order matters:
function subtract(first, second) { return first - second; }Predict:
subtract(10, 3);and:
subtract(3, 10);The first argument always corresponds to the first parameter.
The second argument always corresponds to the second parameter.
So when you see:
subtract(10, 3);you can think:
first → 10 second → 3and therefore:
first - second;becomes:
10 - 3;Functions are not limited to one input.
You can give a function as many parameters as the computation needs:
function someFunction(first, second, third) { // ... }and then provide the corresponding arguments when you call it:
someFunction(10, 20, 30);For now, pay attention to the correspondence:
parameters are the names in the function definition; arguments are the values supplied when the function is called.
What does isEven(12) produce?# Try this in the REPL:
const result = isEven(12);Now:
result;What do you expect?
You should get:
trueThis tells us something important.
The function call:
isEven(12);is itself an expression.
It produces a value.
That means we can use it anywhere we could use that value.
For example:
const result = isEven(12); console.log(result);Or:
console.log(isEven(12));Or:
if (isEven(12)) { console.log("12 is even"); }In all three cases, the function is being called and the value it produces is being used.
Let’s change the function# Look at this:
function isEven(number) { return number % 2 === 0; }What do you think return does?
Don’t look it up.
Instead, experiment.
Change the function to:
function isEven(number) { number % 2 === 0; }Now try:
isEven(12);What happened?
Try:
const result = isEven(12); result;What value did you get?
You should find that the result is:
undefinedNow put return back:
function isEven(number) { return number % 2 === 0; }And try again:
isEven(12);This time:
trueThe return allows the function to produce the value of the expression after it:
return number % 2 === 0;So:
isEven(12);produces:
true;and:
isEven(13);produces:
false;This is why we can write:
const result = isEven(12);The value produced by the function call becomes the value stored in result.
Computing and displaying are different things# There is another problem in our original program.
We have solved one kind of repetition.
Instead of repeatedly writing:
number % 2 === 0;we can write:
isEven(number);But suppose we want the program to say:
12 is even 17 is odd 24 is evenWe might write:
const number1 = 12; const number2 = 17; const number3 = 24; console.log(number1 + " is even"); console.log(number2 + " is odd"); console.log(number3 + " is even");There is repetition here too.
More importantly, there are now two different jobs happening:
deciding whether a number is even; displaying something to the user. Let’s separate them.
First, keep our computation:
function isEven(number) { return number % 2 === 0; }Now write another function:
function describeEven(number) { const description = isEven(number) ? "even" : "odd"; return `${number} is ${description}`; }Now try:
console.log(describeEven(12)); console.log(describeEven(17)); console.log(describeEven(24));What does describeEven produce?
It produces a string.
Try:
const message = describeEven(12);Then:
console.log(message);The function computes a value.
The console.log displays that value.
This distinction will become increasingly useful as your programs get larger.
Ask yourself:
Is this function figuring something out, or is it displaying something?
For example:
isEven(12);figures something out.
console.log(isEven(12));displays the result.
And remember something from the previous lesson:
console.log("hello");does display something, but the function call itself produces:
undefinedSo console.log is useful for its side effect—printing something—not because it gives you a useful value to continue computing with.
Where do the variables live?# You have already worked with lookup tables when drawing expression trees.
For example, if you have:
const x = 10; const y = 20; console.log(x + y);you can imagine a table like this:
Name Value x 10 y 20 When JavaScript evaluates:
x + y;it looks up x and y in the table.
You have already practised doing exactly this with expression trees: look up the names, then evaluate the expression.
Now let’s see what happens when we put variables inside a block.
Try an experiment# Open the REPL and enter:
if (true) { const x = 10; console.log(x); }This prints:
10So x clearly exists when JavaScript evaluates:
console.log(x);Now try:
console.log(x);What happens?
You should get an error.
But why?
We can understand this using the same lookup-table idea.
When JavaScript is inside the if block, imagine that it has another table:
Outside the block:
Name Value Inside the block:
Name Value x 10 When JavaScript evaluates:
console.log(x);inside the block, it can find x in the current table.
When you evaluate:
console.log(x);outside the block, that table is no longer the current table.
There is no x there.
This is what scope means.
A scope is a region of your program with its own set of names.
You can think of it as JavaScript using a different lookup table.
What about variables outside the block?# Try this:
const x = 10; if (true) { const y = 20; console.log(x); console.log(y); }Both values can be printed.
Why?
Think about the tables again.
The outer table contains:
Name Value x 10 The if block has another table:
Name Value y 20 When JavaScript is inside the block and looks for y, it finds it in the current table.
What happens when it looks for x?
There is no x in the block’s table.
So it looks in the outer table.
It finds:
x → 10This is why this works:
console.log(x);inside the block.
But if we leave the block and try:
console.log(y);JavaScript cannot find y in the outer table.
The table belonging to the if block is no longer the current table.
Try changing the table# Try this:
const x = 10; if (true) { const x = 20; console.log(x); } console.log(x);Before you run it, predict the output.
You might expect JavaScript to complain:
“You already have a variable called x!”
But it doesn’t.
The output is:
20 10Why?
There are two different tables.
The outer table contains:
Name Value x 10 The table for the if block contains:
Name Value x 20 When JavaScript is inside the block, it finds x in the current table:
x → 20When it leaves the block, the current table is the outer one:
x → 10So the same name can have different values in different scopes.
The important thing is not that JavaScript has two variables fighting over the same name.
They are in different tables.
Functions have their own table# Now we can apply exactly the same idea to functions.
Try:
function test() { const number = 12; console.log(number); } test();This works.
Now try:
console.log(number);What happens?
Again, think about the tables.
Outside the function, we might have:
Name Value When test() runs, the function has its own table:
Name Value number 12 Inside the function, JavaScript can look up:
number;in that table.
Outside the function, that is not the current table anymore.
So number cannot be found.
This is the same idea you just saw with an if block.
A function creates another scope.
Parameters go into the table too# Look at our isEven function:
function isEven(number) { return number % 2 === 0; }When we call:
isEven(12);you can think of the function getting its own table:
Name Value number 12 Then JavaScript evaluates:
number % 2 === 0;using that table.
If we call:
isEven(17);the function gets a function scope in which:
Name Value number 17 The name is the same.
The value is different.
The function’s parameter is simply another name that exists in its scope.
This gives you a useful way to think about functions:
When a function runs, it gets its own lookup table.
Variables declared inside the function go into that table.
Its parameters go into that table.
When JavaScript evaluates an expression inside the function, it looks for names in the appropriate table.
You don’t need to think about the memory inside the computer or how JavaScript implements this.
For now, keep using the lookup-table model you already know.
A scope is, in effect, a different table of names and values.
Building on functions# Now that we have isEven, consider another question.
How could we write isOdd?
You could calculate oddness from scratch:
function isOdd(number) { return number % 2 !== 0; }That works.
But there is another possibility.
Think about what we already know:
if a number is even, it is not odd; if a number is not even, it is odd. So try:
function isOdd(number) { return !isEven(number); }Test it:
console.log(isOdd(3)); console.log(isOdd(4)); console.log(isOdd(17)); console.log(isOdd(20));Predict the output before running it.
Notice what happened.
isOdd uses isEven.
A function can call another function.
This is one of the reasons giving computations names is useful.
Once you have written a useful computation, you don’t have to write it again.
Other parts of your program can build on it.
A bigger problem: classifying numbers# Let’s try something slightly larger.
Suppose we have two numbers:
const number1 = 15; const number2 = -3;We want the program to tell us whether each number is:
zero positive negative We could start like this:
if (number1 === 0) { console.log("zero"); } else if (number1 > 0) { console.log("positive"); } else { console.log("negative"); } if (number2 === 0) { console.log("zero"); } else if (number2 > 0) { console.log("positive"); } else { console.log("negative"); }Run it.
You should get:
positive negativeBut once again, look at the program.
We have written the same decision twice.
What changes?
Only the number.
The classification itself is the same.
So let’s give that computation a name.
How might we write:
classify(number);so that it produces:
"zero"or:
"positive"or:
"negative"Try writing it yourself before looking at the solution.
Remember that a function can return a value.
One possible solution is:
function classify(number) { if (number === 0) { return "zero"; } if (number > 0) { return "positive"; } return "negative"; }Now we can write:
console.log(classify(15)); console.log(classify(-3)); console.log(classify(0));The result is:
positive negative zeroLook carefully at the structure.
function classify(number) { if (number === 0) { return "zero"; } if (number > 0) { return "positive"; } return "negative"; }The first return does something important.
When:
number === 0;is true, the function returns:
"zero";and the function is finished.
It does not continue to the next if.
If the number is not zero, we reach the next if.
If:
number > 0;is true, we return:
"positive";Otherwise, we reach the final line:
return "negative";This is a useful pattern.
Instead of making one large if/else if/else, you can sometimes ask a question and immediately return when you know the answer:
if (...) { return "..."; } if (...) { return "..."; } return "...";You will see this pattern often.
Keep the computation separate# Now imagine that we want to classify two numbers:
const number1 = 15; const number2 = -3;We can write:
console.log(classify(number1)); console.log(classify(number2));Notice where console.log is.
It is outside classify.
classify does not print anything.
It computes a classification and returns it.
The program decides what to do with that value.
For example:
const result = classify(15); console.log(result);Or:
if (classify(15) === "positive") { console.log("The number is positive."); }The function gives us a value.
The rest of the program decides what to do with that value.
What happens first?# There is one more thing you need to understand.
Consider this program:
function greet() { console.log("hello"); } console.log("start"); greet(); console.log("end");Before running it, predict the exact output.
Write down what you think will happen.
Then run it.
You should get:
start hello endNow let’s make it slightly more interesting:
function first() { console.log("first"); } function second() { console.log("second"); first(); } console.log("start"); second(); console.log("end");Again, predict the output.
Don’t run it yet.
Follow the program from top to bottom.
The output is:
start second first endWhy?
The function declarations themselves don’t print anything.
The program reaches:
console.log("start");so it prints:
startThen:
second();calls second.
Inside second:
console.log("second");prints:
secondThen:
first();calls first, which prints:
firstEventually second finishes, and the program continues:
console.log("end");So:
start second first endOne strange thing# There is something interesting about function declarations.
Try this:
greet(); function greet() { console.log("hello"); }What do you expect?
Run it.
It works.
The function is declared after the call, but JavaScript still allows this form of function declaration to be called.
You don’t need to worry about how JavaScript makes this possible.
For now, there is a more useful convention:
Write your function declarations before the code that uses them.
So prefer:
function greet() { console.log("hello"); } greet();rather than:
greet(); function greet() { console.log("hello"); }It makes the program easier to read.
You will encounter another way of creating functions later. For now, stick to the function syntax you have learned today.
Exercises# For each exercise, create a separate JavaScript file.
Don’t put all the exercises into one file.
For every exercise, first try to predict what your program will do. Then run it and compare the result with your prediction.
1. isPositive# Write a function:
isPositive(number);that returns true when the number is greater than zero and false otherwise.
Test it with several numbers.
Try:
10 -10 0 1 -1 2. isZero# Write:
isZero(number);It should return true when the number is zero and false otherwise.
Test it with at least five numbers.
3. isOdd# Write:
isOdd(number);Do not repeat the divisibility calculation from isEven.
Use the function you already wrote.
For example:
function isOdd(number) { // ... }Test your function.
4. absolute# Write a function:
absolute(number);It should return the positive version of a number.
For example:
absolute(10) → 10 absolute(-10) → 10 absolute(0) → 0Think about the different cases before writing the function.
5. describeNumber# Write:
describeNumber(number);It should return one of:
"zero" "positive" "negative"Do not print from inside the function.
Test it like this:
console.log(describeNumber(10)); console.log(describeNumber(-10)); console.log(describeNumber(0)); 6. Use a function inside another function# Write:
isNonZero(number);It should return true when a number is not zero.
Use your isZero function.
Do not repeat the comparison with zero inside isNonZero.
7. String length# You already know that strings have a .length.
Write:
isLong(word);It should return true when the string contains more than 5 characters.
For example:
isLong("hello") → false isLong("elephant") → trueYou only need .length. You do not need any new string methods.
8. Describe a word# Write:
describeWord(word);It should return:
"empty"when the string has length 0, and:
"non-empty"otherwise.
Test it with several strings.
9. Predict the output# Do not run this program yet.
Write down the exact order in which the words will be printed.
function first() { console.log("A"); } function second() { console.log("B"); first(); console.log("C"); } console.log("D"); second(); console.log("E");What is the output?
Only after you have written down your answer should you run the program.
Were you correct?
10. Trace the program# Again, do not run the program immediately.
function isEven(number) { return number % 2 === 0; } function describe(number) { if (isEven(number)) { return "even"; } return "odd"; } console.log("start"); console.log(describe(7)); console.log(describe(12)); console.log("end");Predict the exact output.
Then run it.
Now explain, in your own words, the order in which the function calls happen.
You have now seen something fundamental about programming:
A useful computation does not have to remain an unnamed piece of code.
You can give it a name:
function isEven(number) { return number % 2 === 0; }and then use that computation elsewhere:
isEven(10);A function can receive a value, perform a computation, and return a value.
Other functions can use that value.
And your program can decide what to do with it.
That gives you a way to take a repeated piece of thinking, give it a name, and build new pieces of thinking on top of it.

title: Const, let, if etc
content:
From the REPL to the Editor# So far, you have been programming in the REPL.
You have typed expressions such as:
5 + 3;and:
10 > 5 && 20 < 30;JavaScript evaluates them and the REPL shows you the result.
You have also spent time drawing expression trees.
You have learned to look at an expression, break it into smaller expressions, and follow the order in which those expressions are evaluated.
Now we are going to change something.
We are going to leave the REPL.
We are going to write a program in a file.
And this raises an interesting question:
What is the difference between typing JavaScript into the REPL and putting JavaScript into a file?
Let’s find out.
Setting up VS Code# We are going to write our first program in a file.
For this, we will use VS Code.
Before we start writing JavaScript, let’s get our workspace ready.
Open VS Code# There are two ways to open VS Code.
From Spotlight# Press:
⌘ SpaceThis opens Spotlight.
Type:
Visual Studio Codeand press Return.
VS Code will open.
From the terminal# There is another way that you will find yourself using often.
Open your terminal and go to:
workspace/intro_jsFor example:
cd ~/workspace/intro_jsCheck that you are in the right place:
pwdYou should see a path ending in:
workspace/intro_jsNow type:
code .What is the .?
It means the current directory.
So:
code .is telling VS Code:
Open this directory as my workspace.
This is a useful pattern to remember. We will continue using the terminal even though we are now writing our programs in an editor.
Look at the left side of VS Code.
You should see the intro_js directory in the Explorer.
This is where we will keep the programs we write during this section.
Creating a file# In the Explorer, find intro_js.
Click the New File button.
Give the file the name:
program.jsThe file should open in the editor.
Now type:
5 + 3;You have just written your first program in a file.
Saving a file# Press:
⌘ SThis saves the file.
You can also save it using File → Save.
Get into the habit of saving after making a change:
write → save → runWe will use this cycle repeatedly.
Now let’s run the program.
Open the terminal and make sure you are still in:
workspace/intro_jsThen run:
node program.jsWhat happened?
Nothing.
You might have expected:
8After all, when you typed 5 + 3 into the REPL, JavaScript showed you 8.
Why didn’t anything appear this time?
Before we answer that, change the program to:
5 + 3; 10 * 4; 20 - 7;Run it again.
Still nothing.
This is an important difference between the REPL and a program.
The REPL has a special job:
Read → Evaluate → Print → Loop
It evaluates your expression and then prints the result for you.
A program does not automatically print the result of every expression it evaluates.
The expressions are still being evaluated.
There is simply nothing telling Node to display their results.
We’ll come back to this.
Running a program# You have already learned something about commands, shells and processes.
When you type:
node program.jsthe shell sees a command.
The command is:
nodeand:
program.jsis an argument given to Node.
Node is a program.
It starts as a process.
It receives program.js as an argument, loads the file, and executes the JavaScript inside it.
So there is nothing mysterious about running a JavaScript program.
It fits the same model you have already been learning:
shell ↓ starts a process ↓ node ↓ receives program.js as an argument ↓ loads and executes the JavaScriptThe fact that the argument happens to be the name of a JavaScript file does not change how the shell starts the process.
This is worth noticing.
You have not left the world of processes and shells.
You have simply given another program something interesting to do.
Giving a value a name# So far, we have worked with values:
20;and expressions that produce values:
5 + 3;But suppose we calculate something and want to give the result a name.
For example:
const age = 20;Before we talk about const, look at this differently.
There is a value:
20and there is a name:
ageWe want JavaScript to remember that:
age → 20What does that remind you of?
Think back to Expression Trees Part 2.
You used a lookup table:
Name Value ──── ───── a 12 b 5 c 3 d 2When JavaScript sees a name such as a in an expression, it can look up the name and find its value.
A variable is a way of putting a name and a value into this table.
So we can think of:
const age = 20;as an expression tree like this:
const / \ age 20Or, using the notation you have already used:
[const, age, 20]When this is evaluated, JavaScript creates an entry:
Name Value ──── ───── age 20Now we have something new.
We have a variable.
A variable is a name associated with a value.
Naming variables# The name of a variable is important.
You could write:
const a = 20;There is nothing technically wrong with this.
But what does a mean?
Compare:
const a = 20;with:
const age = 20;The second one tells a human reader much more.
Names are part of how we communicate through programs.
There are rules about what can be used as a variable name.
For now, follow these conventions:
const age = 20; const totalMarks = 87; const studentName = "Ravi";Prefer camel case:
studentName; totalMarks; numberOfStudents;Start with a letter.
You will sometimes see names beginning with _:
_internalValue;There are legitimate uses for this, but don’t reach for _ just because you don’t know what else to call something.
And $ can technically appear in JavaScript names too:
$thing;You will occasionally encounter this in real programs.
For our programs, you will almost never need it.
Most of the time, a good variable name is simply:
a descriptive word, or several descriptive words written in camel case.
Why const?# Let’s return to:
const age = 20;What happens if we write:
const age = 20; const age = 30;Run it.
JavaScript complains.
Why?
Look at the table.
After the first statement:
Name Value ──── ───── age 20Now JavaScript encounters:
const age = 30;The tree is:
const / \ age 30JavaScript tries to create an entry for age.
But age is already there.
You cannot create another const with the same name in the same scope.
So JavaScript stops and reports an error.
The important thing isn’t the exact wording of the error.
The important thing is what happened to our table.
We already had:
age → 20and const says:
Create this name with this value.
But the name already exists.
const also means something else# There is another experiment.
Start with:
const age = 20;Now try:
age = 30;This is different from declaring another variable.
We aren’t saying:
Create age.
We are saying:
Change the value associated with age.
Think about our table.
It currently contains:
Name Value ──── ───── age 20An ordinary assignment would try to turn this into:
Name Value ──── ───── age 30But age was declared using const.
const does not allow the variable to be reassigned.
So JavaScript reports an error.
The expression tree for the assignment might be thought of as:
= / \ age 30The tree is asking JavaScript to change the table.
But the declaration has said that this particular name cannot be reassigned.
So:
const age = 20;means, roughly:
Create the name age, associate it with 20, and don’t allow age to be reassigned.
This gives us a useful default.
Prefer const# When you create a variable, start by asking:
Do I expect this variable to be reassigned later?
If the answer is no, use:
constThis is why you should generally prefer const by default.
You aren’t telling JavaScript that the value can never exist differently anywhere.
You are telling JavaScript that this variable name will not be reassigned.
But sometimes a value needs to change# Consider a game.
A player’s score might start at zero:
let score = 0;and later become:
10then:
20then:
35We need a variable that can be reassigned.
This is where let comes in.
let# Try:
let score = 0;Think about the tree:
let / \ score 0or:
[let, score, 0]JavaScript evaluates this declaration.
The table becomes:
Name Value ───── ───── score 0Now try:
score = 10;The assignment changes the table:
Name Value ───── ───── score 10Now:
score = 20;The table becomes:
Name Value ───── ───── score 20And:
score = score + 5;What happens here?
Look at the expression tree.
There are really two things happening.
First:
score + 5must be evaluated.
JavaScript looks up score:
score → 20so:
score + 5becomes:
20 + 5which produces:
25Then the assignment updates the table:
Name Value ───── ───── score 25This is very similar to what you did in Expression Trees Part 2 when you followed values through a changing lookup table.
let and declaring again# Now try:
let score = 0; let score = 10;What do you think happens?
Remember what happened with const.
The first declaration creates:
score → 0The second declaration tries to create score again.
That isn’t allowed in the same scope.
So both const and let create a variable.
Both prevent you from declaring the same variable again in the same scope.
The important difference for us right now is:
const → cannot be reassigned let → can be reassignedSo:
const age = 20; age = 21;is an error.
But:
let age = 20; age = 21;is fine.
For now, don’t worry about the word scope.
We will meet that idea when we start putting code inside if statements.
A small program# Let’s put these ideas together.
Create:
program.jsand write:
const price = 50; const quantity = 3; let total = price * quantity;Run:
node program.jsWhat appears?
Nothing.
But something happened.
Try tracing the table.
First:
const price = 50;gives:
price → 50Then:
const quantity = 3;gives:
price → 50 quantity → 3Then:
let total = price * quantity;JavaScript evaluates:
price * quantityby looking up the names:
50 * 3which produces:
150The table becomes:
price → 50 quantity → 3 total → 150The program has done real work.
It just hasn’t displayed anything.
How do we make it display something?# You already know how to ask JavaScript for a value in the REPL.
For example:
5 + 3;The REPL prints:
8But a program doesn’t have the REPL’s Print step.
So we need something else.
Try this:
console.log("Hello");Run:
node program.jsNow you get:
HelloWe’ve just met console.log.
console.log# Try:
console.log(5 + 3);You should see:
8Notice the difference between these:
5 + 3;and:
console.log(5 + 3);The first evaluates an expression.
The second calls console.log with the result of that expression.
You already know about function calls from your Expression Trees work.
Think about:
console.log(5 + 3);as a tree:
console.log | (+) / \ 5 3JavaScript evaluates:
5 + 3first.
That produces:
8Then console.log is called with:
8and the value is written to the terminal.
Try:
const price = 50; const quantity = 3; let total = price * quantity; console.log(total);Now you finally see:
150 But why does the REPL show undefined?# There is one small mystery.
Try this in the REPL:
console.log("Hello");You will probably see something like:
Hello undefinedWhy?
We know that console.log printed:
HelloBut what is the second line?
Remember what the REPL does.
It evaluates what you type and then prints the result of that evaluation.
The console.log function itself does not produce an interesting value for us.
Its result is:
undefinedSo two different things are happening:
console.log("Hello") ↓ prints "Hello" the call itself ↓ produces undefined REPL ↓ prints undefinedThat is why the REPL can show both:
Hello undefinedThe Hello came from console.log.
The undefined came from the REPL printing the result of the call.
In a file:
console.log("Hello");there is no REPL sitting there printing the result of every expression.
So you simply see:
Hello Now we can make a decision# We have variables.
We have values.
We have expressions.
We can print things.
But programs also need to make decisions.
Suppose:
const age = 20;We want to print:
Adultonly if the age is at least 18.
We already know how to ask JavaScript a question:
age >= 18;That expression produces a boolean.
So try this:
const age = 20; if (age >= 18) { console.log("Adult"); }Run it.
You should see:
AdultNow change:
const age = 15;Run it again.
What happened?
Nothing.
This is something new.
Earlier, when we evaluated an expression, JavaScript evaluated the expression.
Here, JavaScript did not necessarily evaluate everything.
It first evaluated:
age >= 18;If the answer was true, it evaluated the code inside the braces.
If the answer was false, it skipped that code.
An if is different# Think back to our expression trees.
For an ordinary expression such as:
5 + 3;the tree contains the parts that need to be evaluated:
+ / \ 5 3For an if, we can think of the structure as:
[if, predicate, then part, else part]For example:
if (age >= 18) { console.log("Adult"); }can be thought of as:
if / \ predicate then | | age >= 18 console.log(...)There is something fundamentally different here.
The predicate is evaluated first.
Suppose:
age >= 18produces:
falseThen the then part is not evaluated.
It is skipped.
This is different from an ordinary expression.
When we had:
5 + 3;both 5 and 3 were needed to calculate the result.
With:
if (age >= 18) { console.log("Adult"); }the code inside the if only matters when the condition is true.
This is the beginning of control flow.
The program is no longer simply evaluating one expression after another.
The result of one evaluation can determine what gets evaluated next.
Adding else# Our program currently says:
If the person is an adult, print Adult.
But what if they aren’t?
We can add another branch:
const age = 15; if (age >= 18) { console.log("Adult"); } else { console.log("Not an adult"); }Now think about the tree:
if / \ predicate then | | age >= 18 console.log(...) else | console.log(...)Or more compactly:
[if, predicate, then part, else part]What happens when the predicate is true?
The then part is evaluated.
The else part is skipped.
What happens when the predicate is false?
The then part is skipped.
The else part is evaluated.
Not both.
This is the important idea.
An if is not merely another way of calculating a value.
It controls which code gets executed.
Try making the decision yourself# Start with:
const number = 10;Can you write a program that prints:
positiveif the number is greater than zero?
Start with only the if.
Then add an else.
Then try:
const number = -5;What happens?
Now try:
const number = 0;Should it print positive?
If not, how would you change the predicate?
Don’t immediately look for the answer.
Write the expression.
Predict what it will do.
Run it.
Investigate.
if and the conditional expression# You have already seen another way of making a choice.
In the REPL you wrote things like:
true ? "yes" : "no";and:
10 % 2 === 0 ? "even" : "odd";This is called the conditional expression, or more commonly the ternary operator.
It looks like:
condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalseFor example:
const result = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";The important word here is value.
The ternary chooses between values.
The result of:
age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";is one value:
"adult"or:
"minor"This makes ternaries useful when you are choosing a value.
For example:
const message = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";This is a good use of a ternary.
When should you use if?# Now consider:
if (age >= 18) { console.log("Adult"); } else { console.log("Minor"); }There isn’t a value we are trying to choose here.
We are deciding which code should run.
That is what if is good at.
A useful distinction is:
Ternary: choose a value.
if: choose which code executes.
Consider this:
const message = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";The ternary makes sense because we are choosing the value of message.
But this:
age >= 18 ? console.log("Adult") : console.log("Minor");is awkward.
We aren’t really choosing between values.
We are choosing which actions to perform.
An if communicates that much more clearly:
if (age >= 18) { console.log("Adult"); } else { console.log("Minor"); }On the other hand, this is unnecessarily long:
let message; if (age >= 18) { message = "adult"; } else { message = "minor"; }We are simply choosing one of two values.
This is a good place for a ternary:
const message = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";So don’t think:
Ternary is short, if is long.
Instead ask:
Am I choosing a value, or am I choosing which code gets executed?
That question will usually point you in the right direction.
One more experiment# Try:
const number = 10; if (number > 5) { console.log("A"); console.log("B"); console.log("C"); }What happens?
Now change it to:
const number = 2;What happens?
Notice that the if controls an entire section of code.
This is another reason not to think of if simply as a fancy expression.
It controls execution.
The expression:
number > 5;produces a value.
That value determines what happens next.
What have we added to our mental model?# When we started, our mental model looked something like:
values ↓ expressions ↓ evaluation ↓ new valuesVariables add a lookup table:
lookup table ┌─────────────┐ │ age → 20 │ │ score → 50 │ └─────────────┘ ↑ │ name lookup │ expressionsconst and let give names entries in that table.
const says:
create this name and don't reassign itlet says:
create this name and allow it to be reassignedconsole.log gives us a way to deliberately produce output.
And if introduces something new:
evaluate a condition ↓ choose which code runsThat last part is particularly important.
Until now, most of our programming has been about:
What value does this expression produce?
Now we can start asking:
What should the program do next?
That is a much bigger question.
Small exercises# Do these in program.js.
Don’t solve all of them at once.
For each one:
Write the program. Predict what it will do. Run it with node program.js. If you were surprised, investigate. 1. A named calculation# Create:
const width = 10; const height = 5;Create another variable containing the area of the rectangle.
Print the area.
2. Change the value# Create:
let score = 0;Then change the score three times.
For example:
0 → 10 → 25 → 40Print the final score.
3. Const experiment# Write a program that declares a variable using const.
Try to declare it again.
What error do you get?
Then start again and try to reassign it.
What is different about the two errors?
4. Let experiment# Create:
let number = 10;Then change it to:
20 30 40Print the final value.
Now try declaring number again with let.
What happens?
5. Even or odd# Create:
const number = 17;Use if and % to print:
evenor:
odddepending on the number.
Try several numbers.
6. Positive, negative or zero# Create:
const number = -5;Print one of:
positive negative zeroYou will need more than one if.
Think carefully about the order in which the decisions should happen.
7. Adult or minor# Create:
const age = 17;Print:
adultif the age is 18 or above.
Otherwise print:
minorTry both an if and an if/else.
8. Ternary or if?# For each problem, decide whether you would use a ternary or an if.
Don’t write the program yet.
A.
Choose "pass" or "fail" and store it in a variable.
B.
Print "Starting...", perform some other operation, and then print "Finished." only when a condition is true.
C.
Choose "even" or "odd" and store the answer in a variable.
D.
Print a warning if a value is outside an allowed range.
Explain your choice.
9. Expression trees# Draw the expression tree for:
const total = 10 + 5;Then draw the tree for:
let score = score + 10;What is different between the two?
What happens to the lookup table in each case?
10. Follow the table# Start with:
let score = 10; let bonus = 5;Then:
score = score + bonus; bonus = score * 2; score = score + bonus;Draw the lookup table after every statement.
What is the final value of score?
Can you trace the entire program using the same table-following technique you used in Expression Trees Part 2?
One last habit# You now have a few more pieces of the language.
But the most important habit hasn’t changed.
When you see:
const total = price * quantity;don’t just read it as English.
Look at its structure.
What is the tree?
What values need to be looked up?
What gets evaluated first?
What happens to the table?
And when you see:
if (score >= 50) { console.log("Pass"); }ask a slightly different question:
Which parts of this program will actually be evaluated?
That is the new idea.
Until now, you have mostly followed evaluation.
Now you are beginning to follow execution.
The REPL helped you learn to ask:
What value does this expression produce?
The editor will now help you learn to ask:
What does this program do?

title: IDE (VSCode)
content:
IDE# IDE stands for Integrated Development Environment.
An IDE is a development environment that brings together the tools needed to write, understand, run, and debug software. It provides a graphical interface that coordinates these tools and makes software development easier.
An IDE helps you:
Navigate code Write and edit code Run code Debug code Search and replace text Manage files and folders Integrate with version control Install extensions for additional functionality For this lesson, we will use VS Code as an example of an IDE.
IDE vs Terminal# We have already seen that when we launch a terminal, it starts a process. Does launching an IDE also create a process?
Let’s look at the process tree of VS Code:
pstree -s "Visual Studio Code"-+= 00001 root /sbin/launchd \-+= 14578 prafullchavan /Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/MacOS/Code |--- 14586 prafullchavan /Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Frameworks/Code Helper.app/Contents/MacOS/Code Helper ... |--- 14587 prafullchavan /Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Frameworks/Code Helper.app/Contents/MacOS/Code Helper ... |-+- 14632 prafullchavan /Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Frameworks/Code Helper.app/Contents/MacOS/Code Helper ... | \--- 14638 prafullchavan /Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Frameworks/Code Helper.app/Contents/MacOS/Code Helper ... |--- 14633 prafullchavan /Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Frameworks/Code Helper.app/Contents/MacOS/Code Helper ... |--- 14728 prafullchavan /Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Frameworks/Code Helper (Renderer).app/Contents/MacOS/Code Helper (Renderer) ... |--- 14729 prafullchavan /Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Frameworks/Code Helper.app/Contents/MacOS/Code Helper ... |-+- 14730 prafullchavan /Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Frameworks/Code Helper (Plugin).app/Contents/MacOS/Code Helper (Plugin) ... | \--- 14781 prafullchavan /Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Frameworks/Code Helper (Plugin).app/Contents/MacOS/Code Helper (Plugin) ... \--- 15625 prafullchavan /Applications/Visual Studio Code.app/Contents/Frameworks/Code Helper.app/Contents/MacOS/Code Helper ...As you can see, VS Code also runs as a process. In fact, it launches multiple processes to handle different responsibilities.
Why so many processes?# When you open VS Code, its main process acts as a manager. It launches different processes, each responsible for a specific job, such as:
Displaying the user interface Handling network requests Running extensions Processing background tasks Managing files and other services Just as a shell can launch multiple processes, VS Code’s main process can also launch multiple child processes.
Key takeaway: An IDE is not just a window on the screen. Like a terminal, it is backed by processes that perform the work. The graphical interface is one way of interacting with those processes.
VSCode is a browser. But how?# If we look closely at VS Code, it looks quite similar to a browser. It allows us to open files in different tabs, switch between them, and interact with different views.
This similarity exists because VS Code uses technologies associated with web applications to build its user interface. It is built on Electron, a framework that allows developers to create desktop applications using web technologies.
However, VS Code is not simply a browser. It is a desktop application designed for software development. It combines a user interface with capabilities such as file management, code editing, debugging, terminal integration, and extension support.
A useful comparison# Browser VS Code Opens and displays web pages Opens and displays code files Uses tabs to switch between pages Uses tabs to switch between files Has a user interface for interacting with web content Has a user interface for interacting with code and development tools Runs web applications Runs development tools and extensions To explore this further, run pstree on Chrome and compare its process tree with the process tree of VS Code.
Think about: Both applications have a main process and supporting processes. What responsibilities might those supporting processes have?
Where Do the Changes Go?# When you edit a file in VS Code, your changes are initially made in the editor. They are written to the actual file on disk when you save the file.
By default, you can save a file using cmd+s.
VS Code also supports Auto Save, which can save changes automatically based on the configured setting. For example, when Auto Save is set to onFocusChange, the file is saved when the editor loses focus.
Important: Editing a file and saving a file are two different actions. Editing changes the content in the editor, while saving writes those changes to the file on disk.
Sections of an IDE# Most IDEs provide several common sections that help developers work with code. In VS Code, three primary sections are:
Editor — The area where you write and edit code. File Explorer — The area where you browse and manage files and folders. Terminal — The area where you interact with the shell and run commands. Different IDEs may organize these sections differently or provide additional sections, such as:
Source Control — To manage Git changes and version control. Run and Debug — To run applications and inspect their execution. Extensions — To install and manage extensions. Search — To search across files in a project. Commonly Used Shortcuts in VS Code# The following shortcuts are for macOS. Shortcuts may differ on Windows and Linux.
Command Palette# Shortcut Action ⌘ + ⇧ + p Command Palette Basic Editing# Shortcut Action ⌘ + X Cut line (empty selection) ⌘ + C Copy line (empty selection) ⌥ + ↓ / ⌥ + ↑ Move line down/up ⇧ + ⌥ + ↓ / ⇧ + ⌥ + ↑ Copy line down/up ⇧ + ⌘ + K Delete line ⌘ + ] / ⌘ + [ Indent/outdent line ⌘ + / Toggle line comment Multi-cursor and Selection# Shortcut Action ⌥ + ⌘ + ↑ Insert cursor above ⌥ + ⌘ + ↓ Insert cursor below ⌘ + L Select current line ⇧ + ⌘ + L Select all occurrences of current selection Search and Replace# Shortcut Action ⌘ + F Find ⌥ + ⌘ + F Replace ⌘ + G / ⇧ + ⌘ + G Find next/previous ⌘ + D Add selection to next Find match Navigation# Shortcut Action ⌃ + G Go to Line… ⌘ + P Go to File… File Management# Shortcut Action ⌘ + N New File ⌘ + O Open File… ⌘ + S Save ⇧ + ⌘ + S Save As… ⌘ + W Close file/editor ⌘ + K, ⌘ + W Close All Display# Shortcut Action ⌘ + B Toggle Sidebar visibility ⇧ + ⌘ + E Show Explorer / Toggle focus VS Code Settings# VS Code provides many settings to customize the editor according to your preferences. You can open Settings using ⌘ + , and search for a specific setting.
Turn on Auto Save# Press ⌘ + , to open Settings. Search for “auto save”. Change the value in the drop-down menu to onFocusChange. Turn off Auto Update# Press ⌘ + , to open Settings. Search for “auto update”. Change the value to off. Increase Font Size to 18# Press ⌘ + , to open Settings. Search for “font size”. Change the value to 18. Hide the Minimap# The minimap displays a small visual overview of the code on the side of the editor.
To hide it:
Right-click on the minimap. Untick Minimap. Move the Sidebar to the Right (Optional)# You can move the primary sidebar to the right if that layout is more comfortable for you.
Right-click on the sidebar. Click Move Primary Side Bar Right.

title: In Defense of Light Mode
content:
I have reached an age at which I have become mildly irritated by the color scheme of my computer.
This is not, I should stress, an important problem.
There are wars, famines, elections, climate change, and JavaScript frameworks that have somehow acquired build systems larger than operating systems. And yet here I am, wanting to talk about light mode.
Because apparently I am now required to defend myself for wanting a white background behind my text.
I like light mode.
There. I said it.
I like black—or nearly black—letters on a light background. I like reasonably large type. I like a room with some actual illumination in it. I like being able to read things without first turning the entire interface into a cave and then discovering that the pale gray text is apparently supposed to be visible.
And I am increasingly suspicious of the proposition that dark mode is somehow better for your eyes.
It may be better for your eyes.
It is not necessarily better for my eyes.
Those are rather different statements.
The Great Dark Mode Revelation# Somewhere along the way, dark mode acquired a remarkable collection of supposed virtues.
It is easier on the eyes.
It reduces eye strain.
It protects your eyesight.
It is better for your long-term vision.
It is somehow more natural.
Perhaps it also makes your coffee taste better.
Some of these claims have a kernel of truth. Some are reasonable hypotheses. Some have achieved the peculiar status of things that are repeated so often that nobody remembers whether there was ever any evidence for them.
The problem is the phrase:
“better for your eyes.”
Better in what sense?
Better for whom?
Under what lighting conditions?
For what task?
For how long?
At what brightness?
With what font size?
And whose eyes?
Because eyes are not identical pieces of consumer electronics.
What Your Eyes Are Actually Looking At# Let’s start with something rather obvious.
A computer screen emits light.
A white portion of a screen emits more light than a black portion of a screen.
So, yes, if I turn my entire screen white, I am putting considerably more light into the room—and into my eyes—than if I turn it black.
But that does not mean that white pixels are slowly cooking my retinas.
This is an important distinction.
There is a substantial difference between:
“This is bright and uncomfortable.”
and
“This is damaging my eyes.”
Ordinary computer displays are not remotely equivalent to staring at the sun. The evidence does not show that normal use of a computer display in either light or dark mode causes progressive retinal damage simply because one uses more white pixels.
There is plenty of evidence that prolonged computer use can produce digital eye strain: tired eyes, dryness, burning, headaches, blurred vision, difficulty focusing and general ocular discomfort.
But eye strain is not the same thing as eye damage.
Your eyes can get tired without being injured.
Your legs can get tired from walking without concluding that walking is destroying your legs.
The same basic distinction applies here.
Then Why Does Brightness Matter?# Because comfort is real.
