The fact that something isn’t damaging your retina doesn’t mean it is pleasant to stare at for eight hours.
The amount of light coming from the display matters. So does the amount of light in the room.
Imagine two situations.
Situation 1# You are sitting in a reasonably well-lit office.
Your monitor is moderately bright.
The text is large.
The contrast is good.
Nothing is reflecting directly into the screen.
Lovely.
Situation 2# It is midnight.
The room is almost completely dark.
You have a gigantic white browser window open at maximum brightness.
Your pupils are adapted to darkness and there is now a luminous rectangle several hundred times brighter than its surroundings sitting in front of you.
This is probably not going to feel wonderful.
The important variable isn’t simply:
WHITE BAD.
It is the relationship between the display and the surrounding visual environment.
The screen should generally be comfortable relative to the room you are in.
This is one reason the “dark mode is healthier” argument is too simplistic. Dark mode may be extremely pleasant in a dark environment because it reduces the amount of light coming from the display.
That doesn’t establish that dark mode is intrinsically healthier.
It establishes that not staring at a blazing rectangle in a dark room can be pleasant.
A surprisingly modest achievement.
There Is Also the Matter of Contrast# Here is where things become particularly interesting.
The human visual system does not merely care about how much light there is.
It cares about differences in luminance.
Text has to be distinguished from its background.
And as we get older, our ability to distinguish subtle differences in contrast generally declines.
This is one reason that:
dark gray text on slightly lighter gray
can be lovely to a designer and absolutely infuriating to somebody trying to read the documentation.
At some point, “subtle” becomes “where the hell is the text?”
High contrast can make text easier to distinguish.
And there is nothing inherently virtuous about low contrast.
A large field of light background with dark characters provides a very strong, familiar contrast relationship.
That is one reason books have historically looked roughly like this:
black marks on something light.
It is not because Gutenberg had failed to discover dark mode.
And Then You Turn 45# Here is where I have to confess that this entire argument has become considerably more personal.
I recently turned 45.
At 25, I could apparently read anything.
A line of code in microscopic gray type?
Fine.
A terminal with tiny characters?
Fine.
A badly designed website with 13 different shades of gray?
Apparently I was invincible.
At 45, I would like the text to be larger.
I would like the contrast to be better.
I would like the room to contain light.
And I would like whoever designed the interface to stop whispering the text at me.
This isn’t entirely psychological.
The eye changes with age.
One of the most familiar changes is presbyopia. The lens of the eye gradually becomes less capable of changing shape to focus on nearby objects. This is why people who have spent their entire lives being able to read at whatever distance they pleased eventually discover that their phone has somehow become farther away every year.
The phone hasn’t moved.
Your arm has merely become part of the optical apparatus.
The lens also becomes less transparent with age, and there is increasing scattering of light within the eye. The pupil tends to become smaller, too. Less light reaches the retina.
At the same time, contrast sensitivity can decline.
So the visual system of a 45-year-old is not necessarily experiencing the same display in the same way as that of a 20-year-old.
This does not mean:
“Everyone over 40 should use light mode.”
It means something much more boring and useful:
Age changes the visual conditions under which an individual finds things comfortable and legible.
And that is precisely why universal proclamations about display modes are suspicious.
More Light Is Not Automatically Worse# There is another amusing complication.
Because the aging eye receives less light, adequate illumination can actually become more useful with age.
That doesn’t mean “make everything as bright as possible.”
It means that the simplistic equation:
less light = healthier eyes
doesn’t work.
For some visual tasks, more illumination improves visual performance.
A well-lit environment can help an older person see.
A sufficiently bright display can make text easier to distinguish.
Higher contrast can make reading easier.
Larger text reduces the demand on visual resolution and focusing.
And suddenly we have arrived at something rather less fashionable than “dark mode is healthier”:
Make things easy to see.
What a radical design philosophy.
The Curious Rise of Dark Mode# Now we arrive at the part of this story that I find rather amusing.
Dark mode did not descend from Mount Olympus bearing a tablet on which the ophthalmologists had written:
Thou shalt henceforth use dark backgrounds.
It became popular for a number of perfectly ordinary technological and aesthetic reasons.
One of those reasons was OLED.
An OLED display does not work like an old LCD display with a single backlight shining through the entire panel. Individual pixels emit their own light. A genuinely black pixel can therefore be turned essentially off.
And this has an obvious consequence:
Black pixels can save power on OLED displays.
If half your screen is black, the display doesn’t have to illuminate those pixels.
On a phone, where battery life is precious, this is not a trivial consideration.
Dark interfaces therefore had a very practical technological justification, particularly as OLED displays became widespread.
Then came the aesthetic justification.
Dark interfaces look futuristic.
Dark interfaces look technical.
Dark interfaces look like you are operating a nuclear submarine.
Dark interfaces make ordinary software appear considerably more important than it probably is.
Developers, naturally, loved this.
Terminal windows had already given us decades of black backgrounds. Code editors embraced them. Then operating systems did. Then browsers did. Then websites did. Then every application on Earth acquired a little crescent-moon icon.
And eventually we arrived at the modern situation in which an application with seventeen settings has a menu containing:
Light Dark System Dim Midnight AMOLED Solarized High Contrast Dracula Gruvbox Something called “OLED Black”
At this point, we should perhaps admit that some of this is customisation for its own sake.
Dark Mode Became a Feature# This is another important part of the story.
Software increasingly stopped telling us how it wanted to look.
Instead, it began asking us.
What theme?
What font?
What accent colour?
Rounded corners?
Sharp corners?
Compact?
Comfortable?
Dense?
Spacious?
Light?
Dark?
System?
High contrast?
Custom?
There is something wonderful about giving people control over their tools.
But customisability also creates a peculiar cultural phenomenon:
If there is a setting, people begin to assume that one of the settings must be objectively superior.
Dark mode is a particularly good example.
It went from:
“Here is an alternative visual presentation.”
to:
“Here is the presentation you should probably be using.”
And then, inevitably:
“Here is why the presentation you should probably be using is healthier.”
That last step is where I become suspicious.
A preference became a feature.
The feature became a trend.
The trend acquired a rationale.
The rationale became a factoid.
And the factoid eventually became something people confidently tell other people about their eyes.
Dark Mode May Be Better. It May Not.# There is nothing wrong with the proposition that dark mode feels better for some people.
It can reduce overall screen luminance.
It can be particularly comfortable in low-light environments.
It can reduce the visual impact of a large bright screen.
Some people find it easier to look at for long periods.
And, on OLED screens, it can reduce power consumption.
All perfectly respectable reasons.
But these don’t add up to:
Dark mode is universally healthier for human vision.
The research on visual comfort and display polarity is not nearly that tidy. Studies have found differences in legibility, visual performance and subjective comfort, but the results are not consistent enough to declare a universal winner.
And that’s hardly surprising.
The human eye is not a machine with a single optimum brightness setting.
Light Mode Has a Rather Long Pedigree# There is also a peculiar assumption that light mode is some sort of antiquated interface convention that we have finally escaped.
It is worth remembering what we spent several thousand years doing.
We wrote things on light surfaces.
Paper.
Books.
Manuscripts.
Newspapers.
Maps.
Letters.
The fact that we don’t traditionally print white letters on black paper isn’t proof that paper manufacturers were conspiring against OLED owners.
Dark text on a light background has an enormous amount of history behind it because it works very well for many forms of reading.
That doesn’t make it universally superior.
It does, however, make the claim that light mode is somehow inherently hostile to the human visual system rather difficult to sustain.
The Problem With “Better”# This is really the crux of the matter.
Suppose I say:
“I find light mode easier to read.”
There isn’t much to argue with.
That’s a statement about my experience.
Suppose you say:
“I find dark mode easier to read.”
Also fine.
Now suppose someone says:
“Dark mode is better for your eyes.”
We’ve changed the nature of the claim.
We have moved from preference to medical proposition.
And medical propositions require rather more evidence.
If the claim is instead:
“Dark mode can be more comfortable for some people, particularly in darker environments.”
Fine.
If the claim is:
“Dark mode can reduce power consumption on OLED displays.”
Fine.
If the claim is:
“Some people simply prefer it.”
Obviously.
If the claim is:
“Dark mode prevents long-term damage to your eyes.”
That is a much stronger claim, and the evidence does not justify treating it as established fact.
So Here I Am, at 45# I have no desire to persuade anyone to abandon dark mode.
Quite the contrary.
If you like it, use it.
If it makes your screen more comfortable, excellent.
If it saves your phone battery, even better.
If you simply think it looks nice, I have no objection.
But I reserve the right to use a bright background, large letters and strong contrast without being told that I am mistreating my eyes.
Because my eyes are 45 years old.
They have started sending requirements.
They would like larger type.
They would like better illumination.
They would like decent contrast.
They would like fewer reflections.
They would like me to stop pretending that tiny gray text is sophisticated.
And, apparently, they would like light mode.
The eyes have spoken.
The Actual Rule# There isn’t a universally correct mode.
There is only a display, an environment, a task and a pair of eyes.
For one person:
dark background + moderate brightness + large text
may be ideal.
For another:
light background + high contrast + large text
may be ideal.
For somebody working at night, the first may be much more comfortable.
For somebody reading dense text in a well-lit office, the second may be preferable.
For somebody with aging eyes, increasing font size and ensuring adequate illumination may become increasingly important.
And for somebody with a particular eye condition, the right answer may be something else entirely.
So perhaps we should stop asking:
“Which mode is better?”
and ask:
“Which mode lets you see comfortably?”
That is a much less exciting question.
It also happens to be the useful one.
As for me, I shall continue to use light mode.
Not because it is medically superior.
Not because dark mode is bad.
Not because I have discovered some secret truth about photons.
Simply because I can see the bloody thing better.
And at 45, that seems like a perfectly respectable criterion.

title: The Kitchen
content:
The Kitchen# Imagine that you are running a busy kitchen.
Not a small kitchen at home where one person makes breakfast.
A very busy kitchen.
There are many people who want to use it at the same time.
One person wants to make tea. Another wants to cook rice. Someone is baking bread. Someone else is making soup. Another person is washing dishes.
They all need things from the same kitchen:
the stove the oven water electricity knives pots and pans ingredients counter space the sink There is a problem.
There is only one kitchen.
There is only one oven.
There may only be four burners.
There is only one sink.
So what happens when five people want the oven?
Or when two people want the same burner?
Or when someone wants to use the sink while somebody else is already washing dishes?
Someone needs to manage all of this.
The Kitchen Manager# Imagine that your kitchen has a kitchen manager.
The manager doesn’t make the tea.
The manager doesn’t bake the bread.
The manager doesn’t cook the rice.
Instead, the manager is responsible for running the kitchen.
Someone says:
“I need the stove.”
The manager decides whether the stove is available.
Someone says:
“I need the oven for 30 minutes.”
The manager decides when they can use it.
Someone asks:
“Can I have some water?”
The manager makes sure they can get water.
Someone tries to take a knife that someone else is using.
The manager intervenes.
Someone finishes cooking and leaves their things all over the counter.
The manager makes sure that the space and resources can eventually be used again.
The kitchen manager is not the person doing the work.
The manager controls access to the resources that everyone needs to do their work.
Keep that person in your head.
We are going to come back to them many times.
The People in the Kitchen# Now imagine that each person in the kitchen has a job.
Alice is making tea.
Bob is baking bread.
Charlie is making soup.
David is washing dishes.
These people are doing different things, but they are all sharing the same kitchen.
Think about the difference between these two statements:
Alice is a person.
and:
Alice is a person who is currently making tea.
The second statement tells us what Alice is doing.
This is a useful way to think about a process.
A process is a program that is currently running.
A program is like a recipe sitting in a cookbook.
It contains instructions, but it isn’t doing anything.
A process is what happens when someone actually takes that recipe into the kitchen and starts following it.
So if you write a program:
make teathe program is the recipe.
When the computer starts executing that program, we can think of the running program as a process.
One Kitchen, Many Processes# Let’s go back to our kitchen.
Alice wants to make tea.
Bob wants to make bread.
Charlie wants to make soup.
All three are working at the same time.
But they are sharing the kitchen.
Alice needs the stove.
Charlie also needs the stove.
Bob needs the oven.
What happens?
Alice might say:
“I need the stove.”
The kitchen manager checks.
The stove is available.
So Alice gets it.
Then Charlie says:
“I need the stove.”
The manager looks at the stove.
Alice is using it.
So the manager says:
“Wait.”
Charlie has to wait until the stove becomes available.
This is one of the most important things to understand about an operating system:
There are many processes, but there are a limited number of resources.
The kernel is responsible for coordinating them.
The Oven Problem# Let’s make the problem harder.
Five people arrive at the kitchen.
All five want the oven.
But there is only one oven.
The manager could arrange things like this:
Bread → Oven Cake → Wait Pizza → Wait Roast → Wait Cookies → WaitThe bread goes into the oven.
The other four people wait.
When the bread is finished:
Bread → Done Cake → Oven Pizza → Wait Roast → Wait Cookies → WaitThe manager has scheduled access to the oven.
This is very similar to what happens with a CPU.
There may be many processes that want to run, but a CPU core can only execute one instruction stream at a time.
The kernel has to decide:
Which process gets to use the CPU now?
And then:
Which process gets to use it next?
Everyone Gets a Turn# Suppose Alice gets the stove.
She starts making tea.
But Alice doesn’t want to give the stove back.
She says:
“I’m going to keep using this stove forever.”
That would be a terrible kitchen.
The manager needs to make sure that Charlie gets a chance too.
So after some amount of time, the manager says:
“Alice, you’ve had your turn. Charlie gets the stove now.”
Charlie cooks.
Then perhaps Alice gets another turn.
The sequence might look like:
Alice → Charlie → Bob → Alice → Charlie → BobOn a computer, the kernel can similarly give processes small amounts of CPU time.
The computer switches between processes so quickly that it can look as though many things are happening at once.
This is part of CPU scheduling.
But How Does Alice Know Where She Was?# There is an interesting problem here.
Suppose Alice is making tea.
She has:
a kettle on the stove tea leaves on the counter milk beside her a cup in her hand She has just started boiling the water.
The manager says:
“Charlie needs the stove. You have to wait.”
Alice leaves.
A little later, the manager says:
“Alice, your turn.”
Alice needs to continue her work.
She needs to know where she was.
She needs to remember something like:
Alice Task: Making tea Step: Waiting for water to boil Tea leaves: 2 spoons Milk: 100 mlA process also has state.
The computer needs to keep track of things about a process so that it can stop running it and later continue from where it left off.
This is part of what happens during a context switch.
The kernel pauses one process, preserves its state, and gives the CPU to another process.
Later, it can restore the first process’s state and allow it to continue.
Running, Ready and Waiting# Now look carefully at what is happening in our kitchen.
Alice is currently using the stove.
She is running.
Charlie wants to use the stove, but Alice has it.
Charlie is ready, but he is waiting for his turn.
Bob has put his bread into the oven.
There is nothing he can do until the bread finishes baking.
Bob is waiting for an event.
These are different situations.
A process might be:
Running
It is currently using the CPU.
Ready
It is able to run, but it is waiting for CPU time.
Blocked
It cannot continue because it is waiting for something else.
Terminated
It has finished.
You can imagine the processes moving between these states:
+---------+ | READY | +----+----+ | | gets CPU ↓ +---------+ | RUNNING | +----+----+ / \ / \ needs resource finishes / \ ↓ ↓ +-----------+ +------------+ | BLOCKED | | TERMINATED | +-----+-----+ +------------+ | | resource becomes available ↓ READYThe kernel is constantly managing these transitions.
What If Bob Needs the Oven?# Suppose Bob’s bread is ready to go into the oven.
He asks:
“Can I use the oven?”
The manager looks.
Someone else is already using it.
Bob cannot continue with that part of his recipe.
So Bob waits.
But Bob doesn’t necessarily need to stand there doing nothing.
He might chop some vegetables.
Or prepare the next part of the recipe.
Similarly, a computer process might ask for something that takes time.
For example, it might ask the disk:
“Give me this file.”
The disk takes some time to respond.
There is no reason for the CPU to sit around doing nothing while it waits.
The kernel can allow another process to use the CPU.
So we might have:
Process A | | asks disk for data ↓ BLOCKED Meanwhile... Process B → CPU Process B → CPU Process B → CPU Then... Disk data arrives | ↓ Process A → READYThis is one reason your computer can continue doing other things while a program is waiting for something.
Asking the Kitchen Manager# There are some things the people in the kitchen cannot simply do themselves.
Suppose Alice wants water.
She cannot rip open the wall and manipulate the plumbing.
She asks the kitchen manager:
“I need water.”
The manager handles the request.
Programs work in a similar way.
A program might need to:
open a file read from a file write to a file create a process communicate over a network ask for memory interact with a device The program asks the kernel to perform the operation.
These requests are called system calls.
You can think of them as the official way for a process to ask the manager for something.
Process | | "I need this." ↓ Kernel | | checks and performs operation ↓ Process | | receives resultThe important thing here is the boundary.
A process does not simply have unrestricted access to the whole computer.
It has to go through the kernel for operations that require the kernel’s authority.
The Manager Makes Sure People Don’t Interfere With Each Other# Imagine Alice is working on a complicated cake.
Charlie walks over and says:
“I’m going to change your recipe.”
That shouldn’t be allowed.
Alice’s work needs to be protected from Charlie.
The same idea exists in a computer.
A process generally has its own memory.
One process should not simply reach into another process’s memory and change whatever it wants.
The kernel provides protection and isolation between processes.
This is important because there may be many completely unrelated programs running on your computer at the same time.
You don’t want your music player accidentally changing the memory belonging to your web browser.
And you definitely don’t want an ordinary program to be able to freely manipulate the operating system itself.
The Kitchen Has a Door# Let’s imagine the kitchen has a locked door.
People outside the kitchen cannot simply walk in and start operating the stove.
There is a controlled entrance.
The kitchen manager controls what happens inside.
The computer has a similar boundary.
Programs run with limited privileges.
The kernel runs with special privileges that allow it to manage the machine.
Conceptually:
PROGRAMS | | requests ↓ KERNEL | | controls ↓ HARDWAREThis is one of the fundamental ideas behind an operating system.
The kernel sits between your programs and the hardware and provides a controlled way for programs to use the machine.
What Is the Hardware in Our Kitchen?# Our kitchen has:
burners an oven a sink a refrigerator knives counters electricity water A computer has:
CPU memory disk network hardware keyboard display speakers other devices The kernel has to manage access to these resources.
The CPU is especially important because it is where instructions are actually executed.
So you can think of the CPU as one of the most important pieces of equipment in the kitchen.
If you have four CPU cores, imagine having four burners.
Four things can genuinely be happening at the same time.
But if you have 100 processes and only four CPU cores, the kernel still has to schedule all of those processes.
What If You Need Another Cook?# Now let’s make our kitchen even more interesting.
Alice is making dinner.
Her recipe says:
“Prepare the salad.”
Alice could stop everything and make the salad herself.
Or she could ask the manager:
“I need another person to make the salad.”
The manager brings another person into the kitchen.
Now we have:
Alice | creates another worker | ↓ SaladThis is similar to process creation.
A process can create another process.
The original process is called the parent process.
The newly created process is the child process.
So we can have a process tree:
Parent / \ / \ Child A Child B | Child COn Unix-like operating systems, processes form this kind of hierarchy.
And you have already seen an example of this without necessarily realizing it.
When you open your terminal and run a command, your shell can create a new process to run that command.
The shell is itself a process.
The command you run becomes another process.
What Happens When the Child Finishes?# Suppose Alice asked someone to make the salad.
Eventually the person comes back:
“The salad is finished.”
The work is done.
The worker can leave.
The manager needs to clean up the resources that worker was using.
The process is now terminated.
But something interesting can happen.
Suppose the child finishes, but Alice hasn’t yet come back to find out what happened.
The manager may temporarily keep information about the finished worker:
Worker Status: finished Result: completed Parent: AliceThe worker isn’t actually running anymore.
It has finished.
But the manager still has a small amount of information about its termination.
When Alice eventually asks:
“What happened to the worker?”
the manager can give her the result and clean up the remaining record.
This is roughly the idea behind a zombie process on Unix.
A zombie is not a process that is secretly still cooking.
It has already finished.
Some information about its termination is simply still being retained until its parent collects it.
What If Someone Needs to Be Stopped?# Now imagine that someone in the kitchen is causing trouble.
The manager might shout:
“Stop!”
Or:
“Leave the kitchen!”
The manager needs some way to communicate with the people working.
Unix has a mechanism called signals.
A signal is a notification sent to a process.
For example, a process might receive a signal asking it to terminate.
Or it might receive a signal telling it to stop temporarily.
The exact signals are something you can learn later.
For now, the important idea is:
The kernel can send notifications to processes.
This gives the kernel another way to control and communicate with the things running on the machine.
The Kitchen Is Always Changing# Imagine looking into our kitchen at one particular moment.
You might see:
Alice → RUNNING Bob → BLOCKED Charlie → READY David → BLOCKED Emma → TERMINATED Frank → READYA few seconds later, everything might be different.
Bob’s bread finishes.
Bob becomes ready.
The CPU becomes available.
Charlie gets a turn.
Alice needs some water.
Alice becomes blocked.
David’s water arrives.
David becomes ready.
A new process is created.
Another process finishes.
The kernel is constantly responding to these changes.
This is what makes operating systems interesting.
A computer isn’t simply:
“Run program A, then run program B, then run program C.”
Instead, there are many independent pieces of work appearing, disappearing, waiting, competing for resources and communicating with one another.
The kernel coordinates this activity.
The Kitchen Is a Computer# Now step back from the kitchen.
We have been talking about:
cooks recipes ovens stoves sinks resources waiting scheduling managers workers messages finishing work But our kitchen is really a model of a computer.
The recipe is like a program.
The person following the recipe is like a process.
The kitchen manager is like the kernel.
The stove, oven, sink and other equipment are resources.
The manager decides:
who gets to use resources when they get to use them what happens when resources are unavailable how processes are created how processes are stopped how processes are isolated what happens when processes finish how processes communicate with the system And the most important thing to remember is this:
The kernel is not doing the work of the processes.
The kernel doesn’t make your tea.
It doesn’t bake your bread.
It doesn’t run your application for you.
It manages the environment in which the applications run.
One Last Question# There is one more thing worth thinking about.
We have said that the kitchen manager is responsible for everything.
The manager controls the kitchen.
The manager decides who gets the stove.
The manager decides who gets the oven.
The manager decides who gets to use the sink.
But ask yourself:
Who manages the kitchen manager?
If the kernel is software, and software needs a CPU to run…
how does the kernel get started?
Who gives the kernel control of the computer?
Who starts the first process?
And if the kernel is responsible for managing processes, is the kernel itself a process?
Don’t worry if you don’t know the answers yet.
Those questions lead us to the next layer of the story: how a computer starts, how the kernel gets control of the hardware, and how the first process comes into existence.

title: Intro to JS part 2
content:
Strings can have properties# Try:
"Hello".length;You should get:
5What do you think happened?
"Hello" is a string.
.length asks about something associated with that string.
Try:
"".length;"Hello World".length;"JavaScript".length;Now try:
"Hello\nWorld";What did you see?
The \n represents a newline.
You can experiment with other strings too.
Try making a string containing:
a quotation mark; several lines; a tab; an empty string. Don’t worry about remembering every escape sequence.
The REPL is available.
A couple of mysterious values# There are two values you’ll encounter often:
undefined;and:
null;Try them.
What does the REPL print?
They both represent some notion of “nothing”, but they aren’t the same thing.
For now, don’t try to force them into a perfect definition.
Instead, try:
typeof 5;typeof true;typeof "Hello";typeof undefined;What does typeof seem to do?
Try:
typeof null;Wait.
What?
If you got:
"object"you have just encountered one of JavaScript’s famous historical oddities.
You don’t need to fix it.
You don’t need to memorize an elaborate explanation.
Just remember that programming languages, like everything else humans build, sometimes carry strange historical decisions forward.
Try:
typeof NaN;What do you think you’ll get?
Truthiness# We have seen values such as:
true; false;But JavaScript can also ask whether other values behave like true or false.
Let’s investigate.
Try:
Boolean(true);Boolean(false);Now:
Boolean(1);Boolean(0);What about:
Boolean("Hello");and:
Boolean("");Try:
Boolean(null);Boolean(undefined);Boolean(NaN);There is a pattern here.
Some values are truthy.
Some values are falsy.
You don’t need to memorize the entire list yet.
Instead, explore.
What about:
Boolean(-1);Boolean(100);Boolean("0");Boolean("false");That last pair is worth thinking about.
The string "0" contains the character 0.
The string "false" contains the word false.
But they are still strings.
So what do you think JavaScript will consider them?
Run them.
Choosing between values# We’ve now got enough pieces to do something interesting.
Try:
true ? "yes" : "no";You should get:
"yes"Now:
false ? "yes" : "no";What happened?
The general form is:
condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse;Try:
5 > 3 ? "yes" : "no";And:
5 < 3 ? "yes" : "no";Now make your own.
For example:
10 % 2 === 0 ? "even" : "odd";Try changing the number.
Can you make an expression that tells you whether another number is positive or negative?
What about whether a number is greater than 100?
You now have enough pieces to make surprisingly complicated expressions without having created a single variable.
That’s intentional.
What about the bits?# There is another family of operators we should briefly encounter.
Try:
5 & 3;Then:
5 | 3;Then:
5 ^ 3;These are bitwise operators.
They’re operating on the bits that make up the number.
You don’t need to become an expert in binary arithmetic right now.
But try:
5 << 1;and:
5 >> 1;Can you find a relationship between the result and the original number?
Try several values.
1 << 1; 2 << 1; 4 << 1; 8 << 1;What is happening?
Now try:
8 >> 1; 16 >> 1; 32 >> 1;Can you discover the pattern?
This is another useful way of learning programming:
notice a pattern before someone gives you the rule.
You may not fully understand what’s happening yet.
That’s okay.
You have somewhere to experiment.
A small challenge# At this point, don’t read the answer to this section immediately.
Use the REPL.
See if you can work these out.
1. What does this produce?# 2 + 3 * 4;2. How could you make it produce 20?# 3. What does this produce?# 10 % 3;4. Can you write an expression that produces true when 10 is greater than 5?# 5. Can you combine two comparisons using &&?# 6. Can you write an expression that produces "even" or "odd" depending on whether a number is even?# 7. What is the length of:# "Hello, JavaScript!";Don’t calculate it yourself.
Ask JavaScript.
8. What happens here?# "5" + 5;And here?
5 + 5;Why are the results different?
9. What happens here?# 5 === "5";Why?
10. Can you construct one expression containing:# arithmetic; a comparison; && or ||; and a conditional expression? It doesn’t have to be useful.
It just has to work.
One last thing# You may have noticed something.
We have spent this entire session evaluating expressions.
We haven’t written a program.
We haven’t created a variable.
We haven’t used let.
We haven’t used const.
That is deliberate.
It is tempting to jump immediately into:
let score = 10;and start building things.
But there’s something more fundamental that we want to understand first.
When you type:
5 + 3;JavaScript evaluates an expression.
The expression produces a value.
That value can be used as part of another expression.
And that expression can produce another value.
So far, we’ve seen:
values ↓ expressions ↓ evaluation ↓ new values ↓ larger expressions ↓ new valuesThis is the basic game.
We’ve been playing it directly in the REPL.
Soon we’ll want to give values names.
We’ll want to keep them around.
We’ll want to make decisions, repeat things, and eventually build programs.
But before we do that, get comfortable with this:
Look at an expression. Predict its value. Ask JavaScript to evaluate it. If you’re surprised, investigate why.
That’s programming.

title: Intro to JS
content:
Your first language# Until now, you’ve been talking to your computer through the shell.
You’ve typed commands. The shell has interpreted those commands, started processes, connected them together, and shown you their output.
Now we’re going to learn a programming language.
We’re going to start with JavaScript.
And we’re going to do something slightly different from what you might expect from a programming class.
For now, we’re not going to write a program.
We’re going to have a conversation.
Open Ghostty.
JavaScript# JavaScript was created in the 1990s, originally as a language for making web pages interactive. Since then, it has grown far beyond the browser.
Today, JavaScript can be used for servers, command-line programs, desktop applications, tooling, and much more.
But JavaScript itself isn’t a program sitting on your computer waiting for you to type things into it.
A programming language needs something that can understand the language and execute it.
That something is an implementation of the language.
There are several implementations of JavaScript. The browser you’re using has one. Node.js has another. Other environments have their own implementations.
For this course, we’ll use Node.js.
You don’t need to worry too much about the distinction yet. Just remember:
JavaScript is the language. Node.js is one implementation of that language.
And Node gives us something particularly useful for learning:
a REPL.
Your first REPL# In Ghostty, type:
nodeYou should see something like:
Welcome to Node.js ... Type ".help" for more information. >That > is Node waiting for you.
Type:
5;Press Enter.
You should get:
5And then another prompt:
>You just had your first conversation with JavaScript.
But what exactly happened?
REPL# REPL stands for:
Read – Evaluate – Print – Loop
Node reads what you type.
It evaluates it as JavaScript.
It prints the result.
And then it waits for you to do it again.
Let’s try something more interesting.
5 + 3;You should get:
8Now try:
5 * 3;And:
20 / 4;And:
20 - 7;The REPL is a little bit like your shell.
You type something, press Enter, and something happens.
But there is an important difference.
When you were using the shell, you were giving the shell commands.
Here, you’re giving Node JavaScript.
Try this:
ls;What happens?
Try:
pwd;What happens?
Now press Ctrl-D to leave Node and return to your shell.
Try:
lsWhat happened this time?
This is an important distinction to get comfortable with:
The shell and the JavaScript REPL may both live inside your terminal, but they are different environments that understand different languages.
Start Node again:
nodeWe’ll stay here for a while.
Values# Let’s start with something very simple.
Type:
5;JavaScript gives you:
5Now try:
42;Then:
-10;Then:
3.14159;These are all numbers.
But there’s something more fundamental going on.
5 is a value.
A value is, roughly speaking, a thing that JavaScript can work with.
And an expression is something JavaScript can evaluate to produce a value.
For example:
5;is an expression.
Its value is:
5And:
5 + 3;is also an expression.
Its value is:
8Keep that idea in your head.
An expression produces a value.
We’ll keep coming back to it.
Numbers# Let’s explore numbers a little.
Try these one at a time:
0; 1; 100 - 100; 5.25;Now try:
1e6;What did you get?
What about:
1e-3;You don’t need to remember every way of writing a number right now. The interesting thing is that JavaScript gives you several ways to describe the same general kind of value.
Now let’s do some arithmetic.
5 + 3;5 - 3;5 * 3;5 / 3;5 % 3;What do you think % means?
Don’t look it up yet.
Try different numbers.
10 % 2;10 % 3;10 % 4;Can you figure out what it is doing?
You may not be able to explain it yet.
That’s fine.
One of the most useful skills you can develop as a programmer is learning to ask the computer questions.
You don’t always need to know the answer before you start investigating.
Try:
2 ** 8;What happened?
What do you think ** means?
Try a few more.
2 ** 3; 3 ** 2; 10 ** 2; Can an expression contain another expression?# Consider:
2 + 3 * 5;Before you press Enter, predict the answer.
Is it:
25or:
17Try it.
Now try:
(2 + 3) * 5;Why did the answer change?
Try:
2 + 3 * 5;What happens?
Now try:
10 - 2 * 3;and:
(10 - 2) * 3;There is a rule here.
JavaScript has rules about which parts of an expression get evaluated first.
You don’t need to memorize all of those rules right now.
Instead, experiment.
Try to find out what happens with:
2 + 3 * 4;(2 + 3) * 4;2 * 3 + 4 * 5;20 / (2 + 3);Can you predict the answer before running each one?
This is the beginning of learning to read code.
Eventually, when you see an expression, you shouldn’t have to run it to know what it means.
But for now, run it.
What else can be a value?# Numbers aren’t the only things JavaScript can work with.
Try:
true;and:
false;These are boolean values.
A boolean can have one of two values:
true falseNow ask JavaScript a question.
Try:
5 > 3;What did you get?
Try:
5 < 3;And:
5 === 5;And:
5 === 10;Something interesting is happening.
The expression:
5 > 3;produces a value.
That value is:
true;So comparisons are expressions too.
They take values and produce another value.
Try:
10 >= 10;10 > 10;10 <= 10;10 != 20;Now investigate this:
5 === "5";What happened?
And now:
5 == "5";Something strange?
Don’t worry if you don’t yet understand why.
In fact, this is a good moment to develop a habit:
When JavaScript does something surprising, don’t immediately memorize the rule. Investigate it.
We’ll return to this later.
For now, prefer === when you mean “are these exactly equal?”
Combining questions# We can also combine boolean expressions.
Try:
true && true;Then:
true && false;Then:
false && false;What does && appear to mean?
Now try:
true || false;false || false;true || true;What about !?
!true;!false;You can now put these ideas together.
Try:
5 > 3 && 10 < 20;And:
5 < 3 || 10 < 20;And:
!(5 === 5);Notice the structure.
We have expressions inside expressions.
5 > 3produces a boolean.
That boolean can become part of:
5 > 3 && 10 < 20;which itself produces another boolean.
This is a pattern you’ll see constantly in programming:
Small expressions can be combined to make larger expressions.
Strings# Let’s meet another kind of value.
Try:
"Hello";You can also write:
"Hello";And:
`Hello`;All three describe strings.
Try:
"Hello" + " World";What did you get?
The + operator can do arithmetic with numbers:
5 + 3;But with strings, it can mean something different:
"Hello" + " World";It joins them together.
Now try:
"Score: " + 10;What happened?
JavaScript is willing to convert the number so that it can combine it with the string.
Now try:
`Score: ${10}`;This is a template string.
The ${...} part lets us put an expression inside the string.
Try changing it:
`The answer is ${5 + 3}`;And:
`2 multiplied by 10 is ${2 * 10}`;Pause here.
What do you think ${...} is doing?
Can you put a comparison inside it?
Try:
`Is 10 greater than 5? ${10 > 5}`;The important thing isn’t memorizing template strings.
It’s noticing that expressions can appear inside other expressions.

Infinity; // Positive infinity. -Infinity; // Negative infinity. NaN; // Represents "Not a Number". // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- // Booleans // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- true; // Boolean true. false; // Boolean false. // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- // Strings // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- ""; // The empty string. "Hello"; // Double-quoted string. 'Hello'; // Single-quoted string. `Hello`; // Template string using backticks. "Hello\nWorld"; // Escape sequences insert special characters. // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- // Other Primitive Values // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- undefined; // Represents the absence of a value. null; // Represents an intentional empty value. // ============================================================================ // VARIABLES // ============================================================================ let score = 0; // Declare a mutable variable. let lives = 3; // Variables can be declared independently. score = 100; // Variables can be reassigned. score = score + 1; // Variables can use their current value. lives = lives - 1; // Updating a variable is a common operation. const width = 800; // Declare an immutable variable. const height = 600; // Constants cannot be reassigned. // ============================================================================ // ARITHMETIC OPERATORS // ============================================================================ // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- // Binary Arithmetic // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- 5 + 3; // Addition. 5 - 3; // Subtraction. 5 * 3; // Multiplication. 5 / 2; // Division can produce decimals. 5 % 2; // Remainder after division. 2 ** 8; // Exponentiation (2 raised to the power of 8). // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- // Unary Arithmetic // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- let x = 5; +x; // Unary plus converts a value to a number. -x; // Unary minus negates a number. ++x; // Increment before the expression is evaluated. x++; // Increment after the expression is evaluated. --x; // Decrement before the expression is evaluated. x--; // Decrement after the expression is evaluated. // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- // Compound Assignment // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- let y = 10; y += 5; // Equivalent to y = y + 5. y -= 2; // Equivalent to y = y - 2. y *= 3; // Equivalent to y = y * 3. y /= 4; // Equivalent to y = y / 4. y %= 2; // Equivalent to y = y % 2. y **= 3; // Equivalent to y = y ** 3. // ============================================================================ // COMPLEX ARITHMETIC EXPRESSIONS // ============================================================================ 2 + 3 * 5; // Multiplication happens before addition (17). (2 + 3) * 5; // Parentheses change the order of evaluation (25). 10 - 2 * 3; // Multiplication happens before subtraction (4). (10 - 2) * 3; // Parentheses force subtraction first (24). 20 / 2 + 5; // Division happens before addition (15). 20 / (2 + 3); // Parentheses change the divisor (4). 2 * 3 + 4 * 5; // Operators of the same precedence are evaluated left to right (26). (2 * (3 + 4)) * 5; // Parentheses can be nested. 2 ** 3 * 4; // Exponentiation happens before multiplication (32). 2 * 3 ** 4; // Exponentiation has higher precedence than multiplication (162). -(2 + 3); // Unary minus applies to the grouped expression (-5). -2 ** 2; // Exponentiation happens before unary minus (-4). (-2) ** 2; // Parentheses make the negative number the base (4). // ============================================================================ // COMPARISON OPERATORS // ============================================================================ 5 == "5"; // Loose equality converts values before comparing. 5 != "6"; // Loose inequality also performs type coercion. 5 === 5; // Strict equality compares both type and value. 5 !== "5"; // Strict inequality compares both type and value. 5 < 10; // Less than. 5 > 2; // Greater than. 5 <= 5; // Less than or equal. 5 >= 5; // Greater than or equal. // ============================================================================ // BOOLEAN OPERATORS // ============================================================================ !true; // Logical NOT inverts a boolean. true && false; // Logical AND requires both operands to be true. true || false; // Logical OR requires at least one operand to be true. 5 > 3 && 10 < 20; // Boolean expressions can be combined with AND. 5 < 3 || 10 < 20; // OR succeeds if either expression is true. !(5 === 5); // NOT negates the result of an expression. // ============================================================================ // BITWISE OPERATORS // ============================================================================ 5 & 3; // Bitwise AND. 5 | 3; // Bitwise OR. 5 ^ 3; // Bitwise XOR. ~5; // Bitwise NOT. 5 << 1; // Shift bits left by one position. 5 >> 1; // Arithmetic right shift. 5 >>> 1; // Logical right shift. // ============================================================================ // ASSIGNMENT OPERATORS // ============================================================================ let value = 10; value = 20; // Replace the current value. value &&= 30; // Assign only if the current value is truthy. value ||= 40; // Assign only if the current value is falsy. let answer = null; answer ??= 42; // Assign only if the value is null or undefined. // ============================================================================ // TYPE OPERATOR // ============================================================================ typeof 5; // Evaluates to "number". typeof true; // Evaluates to "boolean". typeof "Hello"; // Evaluates to "string". typeof undefined; // Evaluates to "undefined". typeof null; // Evaluates to "object" (historical JavaScript quirk). typeof NaN; // NaN is still a number. // ============================================================================ // TRUTHINESS // ============================================================================ Boolean(true); // true remains true. Boolean(false); // false remains false. Boolean(1); // Non-zero numbers are truthy. Boolean(0); // Zero is falsy. Boolean("Hello"); // Non-empty strings are truthy. Boolean(""); // The empty string is falsy. Boolean(null); // null is falsy. Boolean(undefined); // undefined is falsy. Boolean(NaN); // NaN is falsy. // ============================================================================ // CONDITIONAL EXPRESSIONS // ============================================================================ true ? "yes" : "no"; // Chooses between two values. 5 > 3 ? 1 : 0; // The condition may be any boolean expression. // ============================================================================ // STRING OPERATIONS // ============================================================================ "Hello" + " World"; // Strings can be concatenated. "Score: " + 10; // Non-strings are converted automatically. `Score: ${10}`; // Template strings support interpolation. "Hello\nWorld"; // Escape sequences create special characters. "JavaScript".length; // Strings have useful properties.

title: Commands
content:
Commands# We’ve seen that the shell reads what we type and either handles it itself or starts another process.
But what exactly are we typing?
ls -l ~/DownloadsThis is a command.
Let’s take it apart.
The Anatomy of a Command# A command generally starts with a command name.
lsHere, ls is the name of the program we want to run.
We can provide additional information to the command using arguments and options.
ls -l ~/DownloadsHere:
ls command -l option ~/Downloads argumentAn option is sometimes called a flag or a switch. Options change how a command behaves.
Arguments provide information to the command about what we want it to operate on.
For example:
ls ~/Downloadsmeans “list the contents of ~/Downloads.”
And:
ls -l ~/Downloadsasks ls to give us a more detailed listing.
The exact meaning of options and arguments depends on the command. Fortunately, we don’t have to memorise everything.
We’ll see how to find out what a command does shortly.
Spaces Matter# There is one small but important detail about commands.
The shell uses spaces to separate the different parts of a command.
For example:
ls ~/Downloadscontains two pieces:
ls ~/DownloadsWhat if a filename contains a space?
Suppose we have a directory called:
My NotesIf we type:
ls My Notesthe shell sees three pieces:
ls My NotesIt does not know that My Notes is supposed to be one argument.
We can tell the shell that the space is part of the argument by putting the argument in quotes:
ls "My Notes"Now the shell treats My Notes as one argument.
This distinction is important because the shell processes the command line before the program receives it.
The ls program doesn’t receive the original string:
ls "My Notes"It receives the command and its arguments after the shell has interpreted them.
We’ll encounter more examples of the shell doing this kind of work later.
A Few Commands# Let’s learn a small collection of commands.
You don’t need to memorise these. We’ll use them to explore the computer.
pwd# pwd tells us where we currently are.
pwdThink of it as:
Where am I?
ls# ls lists the contents of the current directory.
lsYou can also give it a directory to list:
ls ~/Downloadscd# cd changes the directory we’re currently in.
cd ~/DownloadsThink of it as:
Take me there.
Remember that cd is handled directly by the shell. It needs to change the shell’s own current directory.
mkdir# mkdir creates a directory.
mkdir playgroundtouch# touch can be used to create an empty file.
touch hello.txtNow:
lsshould show hello.txt.
echo# echo prints something.
echo helloTry:
echo "Hello, world."You’ll see the text printed back to you.
clear# clear clears the terminal screen.
clearThere are also keyboard shortcuts for controlling the terminal. On our systems, Ctrl-L is a convenient way of clearing/redrawing the screen.
You may see keyboard shortcuts such as ^L or ^K written down. The ^ notation means Ctrl: ^L means Ctrl-L.
man# Finally, one of the most useful commands of all:
man lsThis displays the manual for ls.
Try:
man mkdirand:
man cdYou don’t need to understand everything in these pages. They’re reference material. When you encounter a command you don’t know, the manual is often the first place to look.
Many commands also provide a shorter help message using:
pstree -hThe command line is not something you are expected to memorise. Learning how to find out what a command does is much more useful.
Let’s Make a Sandbox# We’re now going to use these commands to explore one of the most important ideas in the command line: paths.
Rather than explain paths with a diagram, let’s make a little filesystem of our own.
Start in your home directory:
cd ~You can check where you are with:
pwdNow create a directory called sandbox and enter it:
mkdir sandbox cd sandboxCheck again:
pwdYou should now be inside your new sandbox.
Let’s make some directories:
mkdir books music mkdir books/fiction books/non-fiction mkdir music/rock music/jazzAnd some files:
touch books/fiction/dune.txt touch books/non-fiction/unix.txt touch music/rock/beatles.txt touch music/jazz/miles.txtWe have now created something like this:
sandbox ├── books │ ├── fiction │ │ └── dune.txt │ └── non-fiction │ └── unix.txt └── music ├── rock │ └── beatles.txt └── jazz └── miles.txtDon’t worry if the diagram looks a little complicated. We’re going to walk around it.
Relative Paths# We are currently in:
sandboxLet’s move into books:
cd booksNow:
pwdWe’re in books.
Move into fiction:
cd fiction pwdNow let’s go back:
cd .. pwdWe are back in books.
.. means the directory above the one we’re currently in.
So from books/fiction:
cd ..takes us to:
booksWe can go up more than one level:
cd .. pwdWe’re back in sandbox.
We can also describe a route in one go.
From sandbox, try:
cd music/jazz pwdWe’ve moved into jazz.
The important thing about this path is that it is relative to where we currently are.
From sandbox:
music/jazzmeans:
Starting here, go into music, then go into jazz.
Try this:
cd .. cd ../books/fiction pwdThe path ../books/fiction means:
Go up one directory from where I am, then go into books, then fiction.
A relative path describes a route from where you are now.
Absolute Paths# There is another way to describe a location.
An absolute path describes a location starting from the root of the filesystem.
The root directory is written as:
/On a Mac, your home directory will be somewhere underneath /Users.
You can see your complete current path with:
pwdIt might look something like:
/Users/your-name/sandbox/books/fictionThat is an absolute path.
Unlike a relative path, it doesn’t matter where you currently are. The path starts at / and describes the complete route to the destination.
For example, from anywhere, you could use an absolute path to reach your sandbox:
cd /Users/your-name/sandboxOf course, you would have to replace your-name with your actual username.
An absolute path is like giving someone a complete address.
A relative path is like saying:
Go upstairs, then turn left.
The second instruction only makes sense if we know where you are starting from.
What Is ~?# Typing your entire home directory is inconvenient.
Fortunately, the shell gives us a shortcut:
~The tilde means your home directory.
So:
~/sandboxmeans:
The sandbox directory inside my home directory.
We can use it from anywhere.
Try:
cd ~Then:
pwdNow go directly back to the sandbox:
cd ~/sandboxFrom there, we can reach our music directory:
cd ~/sandbox/musicNotice that this doesn’t depend on where we started.
Let’s Wander Around# Now try navigating around the sandbox without following instructions one at a time.
Start here:
cd ~/sandboxCan you get to the Beatles file using a relative path?
cd music/rockCheck:
pwd lsYou should see:
beatles.txtNow get back to sandbox using ..:
cd ../.. pwdYou should be back in sandbox.
Can you get to the Miles Davis file using a single relative path?
cd music/jazz lsAnd now, from there, get to the Unix file:
cd ../../books/non-fiction lsFinally, use an absolute-ish path beginning with ~ to return to the fiction directory:
cd ~/sandbox/books/fiction lsThe more you do this, the less mysterious paths become.
There are two basic ways of telling the shell where something is:
absolute path "Start at the root and follow this complete route." relative path "Start where I am and follow this route."And ~ gives us a convenient name for our home directory.
You now have most of the vocabulary you need to start moving around the filesystem from the command line.
The important thing is that you don’t need to memorise a collection of commands. You need to understand what the pieces of a command mean, and know how to ask the computer when you don’t know something.

title: Process, Terminals, Shells
content:
Process# When your computer starts, the kernel is one of the first pieces of the operating system to start running. The kernel is responsible for managing the computer: its memory, CPU, devices, files and, importantly, the programs that are running.
But what does it mean for a program to be running?
From Program to Process# A program starts life as a file on a storage device. When you install an application, its code is sitting on your disk or SSD.
When you open the application, the operating system copies the parts it needs into RAM and asks the kernel to start executing its code.
That running program is a process.
So:
program on disk ↓ loaded ↓ RAM ↓ executing ↓ processYou can see this happening on a Mac without writing any code.
Open Activity Monitor. You can find it by opening Spotlight with ⌘ Space and searching for Activity Monitor.
Activity Monitor shows you the processes currently running on your computer. Some of them are applications you recognise. Many others are background processes that you have never seen before.
Leave Activity Monitor open for a moment and open another application. Watch the list. You should see new processes appear.
Close the application again. Its processes will eventually disappear.
There is much more going on here than a list of applications, though. Processes can start other processes.
PIDs# Every process has a number called a Process ID, or PID.
Look at Activity Monitor again. One of the columns is PID. This number identifies a particular process.
For example:
Application PID --------------------- Safari 3812 Calculator 4271The numbers aren’t names for the programs. They are identifiers assigned to individual processes.
We can explore this relationship more easily from the command line.
A First Look at the Command Line# For the experiments in this section, we need a way to type commands to the operating system.
On a Mac, open Terminal. You can find it with Spotlight in the same way you found Activity Monitor.
You will see a window containing something that looks roughly like this:
your-computer ~ %Don’t worry about what all of this means yet. For now, think of Terminal as a place where we can type commands and see their results. We’ll come back to exactly what a terminal and a shell are later.
Type:
pstreeand press Enter.
pstree displays processes as a tree. You may see something like:
launchd ├── Terminal │ └── zsh │ └── pstree └── ...Your output will be different. That’s fine.
Notice something interesting: pstree itself appears in the tree.
That’s because pstree is a program too. When you typed pstree, the shell started a new process to run it.
This gives us our first useful picture of processes:
shell └── pstreeThe shell is the parent and pstree is its child.
Child Processes# Processes can create other processes.
For example:
shell ├── program A └── program BHere the shell started two programs. Those programs are child processes of the shell.
A process can itself start more processes:
shell └── program A ├── worker └── workerThis is why pstree is useful. Instead of seeing processes as a flat list, we can see their relationships.
Run pstree a few times. Then open another application and run it again. Look at what changes.
The exact output will depend on your computer. The important thing is the shape of the tree.
Signals# Processes can also receive signals.
A signal is a notification sent to a process telling it that something has happened or asking it to perform some action.
For example, when you run a program in Terminal and press Ctrl-C, you are sending it a signal asking it to stop.
You can also send a signal using the process’s PID:
kill 4271Here 4271 is the PID of the process you want to signal.
Despite its name, kill does not necessarily mean “destroy this process immediately.” It is a command for sending signals to processes. Different signals have different meanings.
We’ll see more of this when we start running programs that don’t finish immediately.
Zombie Processes# There is one final oddity worth seeing.
A child process can finish running while its parent process is still alive. When this happens, the parent needs to collect some information about the child’s termination.
If the child has finished but its parent hasn’t yet collected that information, the child can temporarily appear as a zombie.
A zombie process isn’t actually running anymore. Its work is finished. What remains is a small amount of information that the operating system keeps around for its parent.
You may eventually encounter zombies when looking at process trees. Don’t confuse one with a process that is consuming CPU in the background: a zombie has already stopped running.
At this point, the important picture is:
process / \ child child / \ child childProcesses form relationships. They have PIDs so we can identify them, and they can communicate with the operating system through signals.
And, as we have just seen, even the commands we type are themselves programs that become processes when we run them.
Terminals# In the previous section, we used Terminal to run pstree.
But what exactly was Terminal?
It is tempting to think of the black window with the blinking cursor as the command line. It is actually a little more complicated than that.
A terminal is a way of interacting with a computer by typing and receiving text.
Today, a terminal is usually an application running inside our graphical desktop. In this section, we’ll see why that is the case.
A Very Short History# The story starts before computers had screens.
Early computers were large, expensive machines shared by many people. Users needed some way to communicate with them. One of the earliest solutions was essentially a typewriter connected to a computer.
You typed something. The computer received the characters. It sent characters back. The terminal printed them.
These machines were known as teletypes or teleprinters. This is where the abbreviation tty, which you may encounter later, comes from: Teletype.
The idea was simple:
computer ↕ characters ↕ terminal ↕ personThe terminal wasn’t doing the actual computing. The computer was.
Over time, paper was replaced by screens. Terminals became things like the famous DEC VT100: a keyboard and screen connected to a computer, communicating by sending and receiving characters.
Eventually, computers became small and powerful enough to sit on our desks. There was no longer much point in buying a separate physical terminal just to talk to your own computer.
So we wrote programs that pretended to be terminals.
These programs are called terminal emulators.
The terminal window you open on your Mac is one of these.
A Terminal Emulator# Open Ghostty.
Ghostty is a terminal emulator. It provides the part of the experience that an old physical terminal used to provide: a place to type characters and a place to display the characters coming back from the computer.
Ghostty itself isn’t the thing interpreting the commands you type. That’s the job of another program, called a shell, which we’ll meet in the next section.
For now, a useful mental model is:
you ↓ Ghostty ↓ shell ↓ programWhen you type something, the keystrokes travel through this system. When the program produces output, that output travels back and Ghostty displays it on your screen.
This is the basic idea behind a modern terminal.
Why Do We Still Use Terminals?# If computers have had graphical interfaces for decades, why are we still typing commands?
Because typing a command is often a very convenient way to tell a computer exactly what you want.
For example:
pstreeasks the computer to show us a process tree.
A graphical application would need to provide a button, menu or other interface for every operation it supports. A command-line program can expose the same functionality through a short command.
Terminals are particularly useful for programmers and system administrators because they make it easy to:
run programs inspect files manipulate files automate repetitive tasks install software connect to other computers That last one is particularly important.
A server in a data centre might not have a monitor, keyboard or graphical desktop at all. We can connect to it over a network and use a terminal to interact with it.
The terminal therefore isn’t just a relic from the days of giant computers. It is still one of the most useful ways of interacting with modern computers.
Some Terminals# Ghostty is the terminal we’ll use in this course. It is fast, cross-platform and designed to behave like a native application on macOS and Linux. It also supports tabs, splits and other conveniences that make working with multiple terminal sessions easier.
There are many other terminal emulators, including:
Terminal.app — Apple’s built-in terminal on macOS iTerm2 — a popular macOS terminal Kitty — a fast, feature-rich terminal Alacritty — a GPU-accelerated terminal focused on simplicity and performance They look different and have different features, but they all perform essentially the same basic job: they provide a terminal interface for programs running on your computer.
And this brings us back to processes.
When you opened Ghostty, you didn’t just open a window. You started a program. That program then started a shell, which in turn can start other programs.
We can see that entire chain in our process tree.
Ghostty └── shell └── pstreeThere are three different things here.
Ghostty is the terminal.
The shell is the program that interprets commands.
pstree** is a command that runs a program.**
We’ll look at the shell next.
Shell# In the previous section, we saw that Ghostty is a terminal. It gives us a place to type and a place to see the computer’s response.
But Ghostty isn’t actually the thing that understands what we type.
That job belongs to the shell.
Terminal ≠ Shell# When you open Ghostty, you are opening a terminal emulator. Ghostty provides the interface through which we interact with another program.
That other program is the shell.
On our machines, that shell is zsh.
The relationship looks like this:
you ↓ Ghostty ↓ zsh ↓ other programsGhostty deals with the terminal. zsh deals with the commands.
You can actually see this in our process tree:
Ghostty └── zsh └── pstreeGhostty is one process. zsh is another process running inside it. When we type pstree, zsh can start yet another process to run pstree.
The three are different things.
What Is a Shell?# A shell is a program that interprets commands.
If you’ve been following along with Sprint, this idea should feel familiar.
Sprint is essentially an interpreter. It reads an instruction, works out what that instruction means, carries it out, and then moves on to the next instruction.
A shell does something remarkably similar.
The difference is that instead of reading instructions from a map, the shell reads them from us.
We can think of its main loop like this:
print a prompt ↓ read what the user typed ↓ figure out what it means ↓ do it ↓ print a prompt ↓ read again ↓ ...In Sprint, instruction 9 means “stop”. A shell doesn’t normally reach the end after one instruction. It finishes one command and comes back asking for another.
Commands# Try this in Ghostty:
lsYou should see a list of files and directories.
What happened?
First, zsh read the characters you typed:
lsIt then worked out what ls means and ran it.
The command itself has a simple structure:
command arguments ↓ ↓ ls ...For example:
ls -l ~/DownloadsHere:
ls is the command name -l is an argument ~/Downloads is another argument Arguments give the command additional information about what we want it to do.
This is somewhat like the instructions in Sprint.
In Sprint:
1 10 20 30The 1 tells us what operation to perform, while the other numbers provide information needed by that operation.
A shell command has a similar idea:
ls -l ~/Downloadsls tells the shell which command we want, while the remaining pieces provide information to that command.
Does the Shell Do Everything?# Not quite.
This is one of the most important things to understand about a shell.
Some commands are built into the shell itself. Others are separate programs that the shell starts.
Try:
pwdThen:
lsBoth look like commands. But they don’t necessarily work in the same way.
ls is a separate program. When zsh encounters it, zsh finds the program and starts it as a new process.
We can see this happening with pstree.
Run:
pstreeYou’ll see something resembling:
Ghostty └── zsh └── pstreeThe pstree process exists while the command is running. When it finishes, that process disappears.
The shell remains.
Ghostty └── zshThis is the difference between the shell interpreting a command and the shell launching another program.
Built-in Commands# Some commands need to be handled by the shell itself.
Try:
cd ..cd means “change directory.”
This cannot simply be handled by starting another program.
Why?
Because the shell itself needs to change its current directory.
Imagine zsh did this:
zsh └── cdThe cd program could change its directory and then finish. But zsh would still be sitting in its original directory.
Instead, cd is built into the shell. zsh handles it itself.
This gives us two broad categories:
command │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ ↓ ↓ shell handles it shell launches another process │ │ cd lsThis distinction is useful because a shell is not simply a collection of programs. It is itself a program that understands some commands and knows how to launch other programs.
Many Shells# zsh is not the only shell.
There are many different shells, just as there are many different terminal emulators.
Some you may encounter are:
zsh — the shell we use Bash — one of the most widely used shells fish — designed to be particularly friendly and interactive sh — a very old and influential shell They all serve the same basic purpose: they interpret commands and provide a way for us to interact with the operating system.
They differ in their features, syntax and behaviour.
For our purposes, we’ll use zsh.
Back to Sprint# There is a useful way to think about everything we’ve seen so far.
Sprint takes instructions and interprets them:
instruction ↓ Sprint ↓ operationA shell takes commands and interprets them:
command ↓ zsh ↓ operation or another processBut there is one enormous difference.
Sprint’s instructions were designed specifically for Sprint. We wrote the interpreter and defined what instructions like 1, 3, 5 and 9 meant.
A shell lives in a much bigger world.
Its commands can cause the operating system to perform useful work, and many of those commands are actually separate programs.
So when you type:
ls -l ~/Downloadsyou aren’t asking Ghostty to list some files.
You’re typing characters into a terminal. Ghostty passes those characters to zsh. zsh interprets them, finds the ls program, and starts a new process with the arguments -l and ~/Downloads.
you ↓ Ghostty ↓ zsh ↓ ls -l ~/Downloads ↓ ls process ↓ output ↓ zsh ↓ GhosttyThe terminal gives us the window.
The shell understands our commands.
The processes do the work.
